rules.statement: Include an accessibility statement
rules.body_excerpt:
An accessibility statement gives users:

- information about how you’ve addressed WCAG
- information about the technical specifications you’ve tested
- evidence of a commitment to accessibility.

For example, your statement might mention how your agency is working on its implementation of the standard.

Include a page on your site that explains the extent your service or product complies with WCAG.

You can check how the Style Manual measures up to level AA in its [accessibility statement](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/12).
rules.violation_condition: The website or service has no accessibility statement page.

heading_path: Plan blog posts with a specific purpose and structure
rules.statement: Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Need support? Here’s what you need to know
- Become a successful leader
- Get your application in now – time is running out

Break up your post with headings and short paragraphs. Order headings from most to least important. Cover one main idea per paragraph. Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.

Use a warm and conversational tone in your blog posts. This will help you engage with the people reading the blog.
rules.violation_condition: A paragraph in a blog post contains more than 3 sentences.
context_preconditions: Applies to paragraphs in blog posts.

heading_path: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals
rules.statement: Use lower case for 'the' and any prepositions, unless they are capitalised as part of a proprietary name.
rules.body_excerpt:
Treat specific days, public events and periods in history as proper nouns and use initial capitals. Use lower case for ‘the’ and any [prepositions](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/130), unless they are capitalised as part of a proprietary name.

In body text, use lower case for generic terms like the names of seasons –‘autumn’ – and astronomical events such as ‘equinox’ and ‘solstice’. Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.
rules.violation_condition: An article ‘the’ or a preposition in a named day, public event or historical period is capitalised without a proprietary-name justification.
context_preconditions: Applies within the names discussed in this section.
Retain capitals that belong to a proprietary name.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation still applies.

heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for an Australian place name
rules.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for an Australian place name
rules.body_excerpt: Don’t use an apostrophe for [Australian place names](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/134) involving possessives.
rules.violation_condition: An Australian place name involving a possessive is written with a possessive apostrophe.
context_preconditions: The place name is Australian and involves a possessive.
This does not address apostrophes serving other functions within place names.
Names of topographic features (peaks, rivers, bays) are the topographic-terms rule's (33e1b1d457c484c8), so 'Carey’s Peak' is not flagged here as well.
compliant_examples: Mrs Macquaries Chair
Kings Cross

heading_path: Use the landing page or cover to identify the report
rules.statement: Use the landing page or cover to identify the report
rules.body_excerpt:
All reports have a landing page or cover (if printed). Use these to give an overview of the report so people can decide if they want to download or read it.

The landing page or cover also shows the:

- title
- subtitle, if any
- name of the author or editor.

They may also show other details such as the date and the publisher.
rules.violation_condition: A report lacks its landing page or printed cover, or that identifying content lacks an overview, the title, an existing subtitle, or the author's or editor's name.
context_preconditions: Use a landing page for an online report and a cover for a printed report.
A subtitle is required here only if the report has one.
A date and publisher may also be shown, but are not required by this passage.

heading_path: Don’t join words with a slash
rules.statement: Don't use a forward slash between words that retain their separate identities.
rules.body_excerpt: Don’t use a forward slash between words that retain their separate identities. Instead, either use an en dash or reword the sentence. Forward slashes can make it look like you mean to show an alternative.
rules.violation_condition: A forward slash joining distinct words to express a relationship or connection, rather than an alternative or another permitted slash use.
context_preconditions: When joining distinct words to express a connection rather than offering alternatives.
compliant_examples: a Sydney to Brisbane flight
a Sydney–Brisbane flight
violating_examples: a Sydney/Brisbane flight

heading_path: Use ‘0’ before a decimal point for values less than one
rules.statement: Always use a full stop, not a comma, for the decimal point.
rules.body_excerpt:
.59

Always use a full stop, not a comma, for the decimal point. This is the style for Australian content.
rules.violation_condition: A decimal value uses a comma rather than a full stop as its decimal separator.
context_preconditions: For Australian content.

heading_path: Use lines and contrast to help readability
rules.statement: Don't use cell or text formatting to convey meaning.
rules.body_excerpt:
Design tables for readability.

- Don’t use colour as the only way to convey meaning.
- Don’t use cell or text formatting to convey meaning. It can make the table difficult to read. Screen reader users cannot ‘see’ the formatting.
- Use lines where they help people read the table. Short tables need only a line above and below the header row and at the bottom of the table. Longer tables need lines, or shading of alternate rows (zebra shading), to help people follow the alignment across the table.
- Ensure there is not too much white space between columns. This makes the content harder to read.
- A table will take up the full width of the screen when viewed on a mobile phone. This may change the white space between columns and make it more or less readable.

A key benefit of tables is that they help people compare information. This is possible only if tables look the same as one another. Use the same font, and font sizes, rule (line) thicknesses and colour schemes for tables throughout the document.
rules.violation_condition: Cell or text formatting acts as a meaning-bearing code in a table.

heading_path: Quote direct speech in single quote marks
rules.statement: Quote direct speech in single quote marks
rules.body_excerpt:
Single quotation marks are also known as ‘quote marks’, ‘quotes’, ‘speech marks’ or ‘inverted commas’.

Use them to:

- show direct speech and the quoted work of other writers
- enclose the title of certain works
- draw attention to a word you’re defining.

Double quotation marks aren’t Australian Government style. Use them only for quotations within quotations.

Short quotations of direct speech are enclosed in single quotation marks.
rules.violation_condition: Short direct speech or quoted writing lacks quotation marks, outer quotation marks are double rather than single, or a quotation within single quotation marks uses single rather than double quotation marks.
context_preconditions: Use single quotation marks for ordinary quotations and double quotation marks for quotations within them.
Long quotations use block formatting instead of enclosing quotation marks.
Speech in transcripts and plays does not need quotation marks when the speaker’s name precedes it; questions and answers have the same exception.
US quotation-mark conventions in quoted US material may be retained or updated to Australian conventions.
Separate rules govern the boundaries of quotations continuing over several paragraphs and whether titles require quotation marks.
compliant_examples: The opposition leader asked, ‘But where’s the money going to come from?’
He also wrote, ‘The decisions of the department for “major procurement” were always political choices.’
‘Yes, that’s all that happened,’ she replied.

heading_path: Follow the order of precedence for the 3 arms of the ADF
rules.statement: Always use initial capitals when writing the short names of the services:
rules.body_excerpt:
There are 3 arms of the ADF, known collectively as the ‘services’ (‘Services’ inside Defence). When referring to the services, follow the order of precedence established by the [*Defence Act 1903*](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Details/C2021C00371):

- Royal Australian Navy
- Australian Army
- Royal Australian Air Force.

Always use initial capitals when writing the short names of the services:

- Navy
- Army
- Air Force.
rules.violation_condition: A short name for an Australian service is written as ‘navy’, ‘army’ or ‘air force’ without its required initial capitals.
context_preconditions: The words are short names for the Australian services, not generic references to armed forces.
The required forms are ‘Navy’, ‘Army’ and ‘Air Force’.

heading_path: Don’t put a full stop after most abbreviations
rules.statement: Don't put a full stop after most abbreviations
rules.body_excerpt:
Don’t place a full stop after an abbreviation.

There are exceptions:

- when the abbreviation ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark
- for abbreviations of scientific names for [plants and animals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/96)
- for the abbreviation ‘n.d.’(meaning ‘no date’) for the year of publication in references.
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviation is followed by a full stop outside the listed sentence-ending, scientific-name and ‘n.d.’ exceptions.
context_preconditions: A full stop is allowed when the abbreviation ends a sentence and is not followed by another punctuation mark.
Abbreviations of scientific names for plants and animals are exceptions.
‘n.d.’ meaning ‘no date’ for the year of publication in references is an exception.

Shortened days and months (dates-and-time.md, e6385dff056b7d93), the cents ‘c’ (currency.md, eda0ce3d55fe9db4), ‘Co’ and ‘Inc’ (organisation-names.md, eacc25a1ee40c53c) and ‘Hon’ (parliaments-and-councils.md, d1549b327a11a626) are their own pages' rules, so they are not flagged here as well.
compliant_examples: It’s listed as a container of ‘misc goods’.
Have you reviewed the relevant para?
Office of Parliamentary Counsel (n.d.) Glossary, Federal Register of Legislation website, accessed 12 January 2020.
The full name of the company is Sizzling Outback Tours Inc.
Xanthorrhoea glauca subsp. angustifolia

heading_path: Organise heading levels in a logical order
rules.statement: Don't skip heading levels
rules.body_excerpt:
Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.

A complete hierarchy helps people scan the content to find the information they need. Screen reader users need to be able to rely on heading level hierarchy to find relevant content.
rules.violation_condition: A heading introduces a deeper subsection without the intervening parent heading level, such as moving directly from level 1 to level 3.
context_preconditions: Check transitions into deeper heading levels.
Returning from a deeper level to a higher-level heading does not require intervening headings.
compliant_examples:
H1: Apply for a drivers licence
H2: Pass the theory test
H3: Learn the road rules
H3: Book a theory test
H2: Pass the driving test
H3: Practise for the test
H3: Book the driving test
violating_examples:
H1: Pass the driving test
H3: Learn the road rules
H4: Pass the theory test
H5: Practise for the test
H2: Book theory test
H2: Pass the driving test

heading_path: Choose simple words, not complicated expressions
rules.statement: Choose simple words, not complicated expressions
rules.body_excerpt:
There is usually more than one way to express something. Find the simplest, clearest option.

Replace longer words and phrases with simpler alternatives. You can use this table as a starting point.

| Don’t write this | Try this instead |
| --- | --- |
| acquire | buy, get |
| additional | more, extra |
| adequate number of | enough |
| address the issue | solve the problem

 answer the question |
| advising in relation to | advising on, advising about |
| amongst | among |
| a number of | some, many, few

 (or tell people how many there were) |
| approximately | about |
| as a consequence of | because |
| ascertain | find out |
| assist | help, support, guide |
| at a later date | later, soon

 (or tell people a specific or rough timeframe) |
| at this point in time | now |
| attempt (verb) | try |
| cease | stop, end |
| cognisant of | aware of, know |
| collaborate with | work with |
| commence | start, begin |
| concerning | about |
| consequently | so |
| create a dialogue | speak, discuss, talk |
| deliver,

 drive | say what you are doing – for example, ‘increasing’ ... |
| desire | want |
| despite the fact that | although

 (or break up the sentence to avoid this phrase) |
rules.violation_condition: A needlessly complicated or formal word or expression is used where a simpler, familiar alternative would preserve the intended meaning.
context_preconditions: Apply the table's verb-specific recommendations only to the indicated verb uses.
The recommendation against ‘table’ as a verb excludes tabling a document in parliament.
Technical or specialist terms may be used when research shows that the audience uses them; plain language remains the default.
compliant_examples: Email your receipt by 5 pm today to claim the prize.
violating_examples: You are required to disclose financial documentation in a timely manner or you will be deemed to be disqualified from this prize offer.

heading_path: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Naming protocols are complicated, specificity is often more respectful
The issue with general terms and when to use them
rules.statement: The term should always appear as 'Indigenous Australians' in the first instance, always with a capital 'I'.
rules.body_excerpt:
‘Indigenous’ and ‘Aboriginal’ are broad terms imposed on First Australians without consultation. These are not words they chose for themselves.

While the term ‘Indigenous Australians’ is in common use, many First Australians may not be comfortable with it.

Using ‘Indigenous Australians’ to refer to First Australians is relatively recent. Its use became popular through international discussions, where the term ‘indigenous’ is appropriate (with a lower case ‘i’). But it is a blanket term that homogenises a wide array of peoples and cultures. This can cause offence.

Due to the common use of ‘Indigenous Australians’ in our society, there may be times when you can’t avoid the term. It can come up in discussions with government organisations, in the names of some organisations or in grant applications.

If you must use it, remember to only do so when writing generally about Aboriginal *and* Torres Strait Islander peoples. The term should always appear as ‘Indigenous Australians’ in the first instance, always with a capital ‘I’. Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear. Using ‘Indigenous’ alone is inaccurate.
rules.violation_condition: A general reference to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples uses ‘Indigenous’ without first establishing the full term ‘Indigenous Australians’, or writes ‘indigenous’ with a lower-case ‘i’ when it refers to First Australians.
context_preconditions: Apply when the term is used for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples generally.
After ‘Indigenous Australians’ has established the referent, ‘Indigenous’ (capitalised) may be used if the context remains correct and clear.
Lower-case ‘indigenous’ is correct in international discussion of indigenous peoples generally, where it does not refer to First Australians.
compliant_examples:
‘Indigenous Australians’ is a broad term and covers a large array of peoples. Often Indigenous peoples themselves do not identify using this term, they will use their local community, island or language group.
Indigenous peoples also have regional terms that they use for specific geographical locations, such as ‘palawa’ or ‘Noongar’ to name a couple.

heading_path: Choose the right word and spell it correctly
rules.statement: Use 'master degree'.
rules.body_excerpt:
A common confusion is how to write about master level degrees. Common spellings include ‘master’, ‘master’s’ and ‘masters’.

Use ‘master degree’. When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
rules.violation_condition: A generic master-level degree is called ‘masters degree’ or ‘master’s degree’, including plural degree forms, or a specific qualification is named in a form other than ‘Master of [area of study]’.
context_preconditions: For a generic reference, use ‘master degree’ or its plural ‘master degrees’.
When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
compliant_examples: He completed his master degree last year.
Having a Master of Arts helped her gain the promotion.
The university offered several master degrees to postgraduate students.

heading_path: Use tables if they make content easier to read
rules.statement: Don't rely on colour as the only visual means of conveying information in tables.
rules.body_excerpt:
User needs:

- I can change the content without losing information or structure.
- I can find and navigate the content and determine where I am on the webpage.

Fundamentals:

- Tables can be made accessible for all users. The World Wide Web Consortium has [tips for setting up tables](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/tips/).
- You must give a table:
- a title (also called a [caption](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49))
- row and column headings
- information (entries)
- a cross-reference in the text.
- You may also need to add notes below the table to help users understand the information and where it comes from.
- Don’t rely on colour as the only visual means of conveying information in tables.
- Don’t leave cells empty. Use ‘zero’ or ‘nil’ or 'n/a' where there is no data. If it is numeric data, use the numeric zero (0). Only use zero if that is the true value.

WCAG quick reference:

- [1.3.1 Info and relationships – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#info-and-relationships)
- [1.4.1 Use of color – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#use-of-color)
rules.violation_condition: Information in a table is conveyed by colour without another way to identify the same information.

rules.statement: Conclude with 'Yours faithfully'.
rules.body_excerpt:
Keep the initial capital for the title in correspondence when you’re writing to a specific person.

In formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Chancellor’ (or ‘Vice-Chancellor’, ‘Professor’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

In less formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Dear Chancellor’ (or ‘Vice-Chancellor’, ‘Professor’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

Don’t include a comma after these phrases. Australian Government style is to write salutations without punctuation.
rules.violation_condition: Correspondence to an academic closes with a formula other than ‘Yours faithfully’ when formal, or other than ‘Yours sincerely’ when less formal.
context_preconditions: Applies to emails and letters to academics.
Formal correspondence uses ‘Yours faithfully’.
Less formal correspondence uses ‘Yours sincerely’.

heading_path: Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited
rules.statement: But don't space a number and its unit when your expression contains more than one time measure.
rules.body_excerpt:
- 35s
- 6hs
- 15mins
- 5d
- 3wks
- 8mo
- 2y or 2yr
- [There are no non-breaking spaces between numbers and units. There is an ‘s’ after ‘min’, ‘hr’ and ‘wk’.]

But don’t space a number and its unit when your expression contains more than one time measure. Use a non-breaking space between each time value instead.

Never add an ‘s’ to show a plural.
rules.violation_condition: A compound expression using shortened time units contains a space between a component's number and unit.
context_preconditions: Applies when an expression contains more than one shortened time measure.
System-specific data formats may have their own requirements.

heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
rules.statement: Write 'o'clock' only when you quote someone directly or transcribe a recording.
rules.body_excerpt:
- We have extended the closing date to 12 am Friday 7 October 2022.

Write ‘o’clock’ only when you quote someone directly or transcribe a recording. In these situations, use numerals and the word ‘o’clock’.
rules.violation_condition: The word ‘o’clock’ appears in an original time expression rather than a direct quotation or transcription.
context_preconditions: Direct quotations and recording transcriptions may use ‘o’clock’.

heading_path: Compare measurements using the same units
rules.statement: number of decimal places.
rules.body_excerpt:
Make it easy for users to compare quantities. Use the same:

- unit and prefix
- number of decimal places.
rules.violation_condition: Quantities presented for comparison have inconsistent numbers of decimal places.
context_preconditions: Applies to measurements presented for comparison.
Compare decimal precision after expressing the quantities using the same unit and prefix.

rules.statement: Don't say a person is inspirational only because of their disability.
rules.body_excerpt:
- person with a disability
- handicapped person
- handicapped parking
- crippled
- invalid
- incapacitated
- mad
- mute
- deaf and dumb
- deaf person
- blind person
- person without sight

You can cause offence when you do not use respectful language, even if it is well intentioned.

- Don’t say a person is inspirational only because of their disability.
- Don’t write about people as if they are heroes or victims.
- Avoid euphemisms and made-up terms, such as ‘differently abled’ and ‘handicapable’.

People with disability could consider these types of terms condescending.

When you are making comparisons, write:

- ‘person without disability’ – rather than ‘able-bodied’
- ‘sighted person’ for someone who is not blind
- ‘hearing person’ for someone who is not deaf.
rules.violation_condition: A person is described as inspirational solely because they have disability.
context_preconditions: The person's disability is the sole basis for describing them as inspirational.

heading_path: Use lower case following a colon in most cases
rules.statement: If the colon introduces a series of sentences or questions, use a lead-in and colon to introduce them in a bulleted or numbered list.
rules.body_excerpt:
The election was fought on a simple question: which party had the best economic credentials?

If the colon introduces a series of sentences or questions, use a lead-in and colon to introduce them in a [bulleted or numbered list](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/56).
rules.violation_condition: A colon introduces a series of sentences or questions in running text rather than as a bulleted or numbered list.
context_preconditions: The colon introduces more than one sentence or question.
The series should be presented as list items following a lead-in ending in a colon.
A missing colon on an existing list lead-in is handled by the list-introduction rule.
compliant_examples:
They answered the question:
They wrote 23 reports.
Each report took 11 days to write.

heading_path: Complete a sentence with a full stop
rules.statement: Complete a sentence with a full stop
rules.body_excerpt:
Full stops mark the end of a sentence that is not a question or an exclamation.

Following the same rule, use full stops at the end of the last item in a [list that’s made up of sentence fragments](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/56#lists_can_be_fragments_whole_sentences_and_standalone_items).
rules.violation_condition: A completed sentence that is neither a question nor an exclamation lacks its final full stop, outside the stated exceptions.
context_preconditions: Applies to sentences that are not questions or exclamations.
The final full stop of a fragment list, and full stops in stand-alone lists, are lists.md's rule (99dceafd6f56c25d).
Sentences ending in link text still require a final full stop, outside the link.
In government social media, a full stop is not required when the post ends in a URL, a tag or handle, a hashtag, an emoji or a sentence fragment.
Government text messages take a final full stop when they finish with a sentence, but not when they finish with a fragment or sign off.
The page separately excludes full stops from headings, stand-alone lists, page headers or footers, captions and titles.
compliant_examples:
The committee met yesterday. It discussed:
office space
working hours
managers’ salaries.
Warning: there is a high probability of hail in your area. Please take appropriate precautions and stay safe. Time sent: 4:30 pm AEST

heading_path: Use a bullet or numbered list instead of semicolons in a complex sentence
rules.statement: Use a bullet or numbered list instead of semicolons in a complex sentence
rules.body_excerpt:
Complex lists in sentences can be hard to read. If you can’t use a bullet or numbered list, separate list items with:

- commas if the list is simple, such as a list of single words
- semicolons if the list is complex, such as a list of items that already contain commas or conjunctions.

In complex lists, you need semicolons to show what goes with what.

It is almost always better to break a complex list into a bullet or numbered list to make it easier to read.
rules.violation_condition: A complex list remains embedded in a sentence with semicolon-separated items when a bullet or numbered list could be used.
context_preconditions: Applies to complex lists within sentences.
An inline list is allowed when a bullet or numbered list cannot be used.

heading_path: Create a list rather than use ordinals
Ordinals in journals and other publications
rules.statement: Don't use 'thirdly'.
rules.body_excerpt:
The committee responded in 2 ways. They asked for an immediate adjournment of proceedings. Secondly, they sought clarification about their powers to subpoena witnesses.

Don’t use ‘thirdly’. Instead, omit ordinals and write the points as a run-on list in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Thirdly’ is used to sequence points in the content.
context_preconditions: Includes journal-style and publication content where ‘firstly’ and ‘secondly’ may otherwise be used.
compliant_examples: The committee took evidence from peak bodies, unions and the department.
violating_examples: The committee took evidence from, firstly, peak bodies; secondly, unions; and thirdly, the department.

rules.statement: Headings do not have punctuation marks.
rules.body_excerpt:
Phrase lead-ins always end in a colon (:).

Sentence lead-ins can end in a colon or a full stop. Choose one punctuation mark and use it for all sentence lead-ins in your document. If in doubt, choose a colon; it is used more commonly.

Headings do not have punctuation marks.
rules.violation_condition: A list heading has a punctuation mark used as a terminal lead-in mark, such as a colon or full stop.
context_preconditions: Applies when a heading introduces a list.

heading_path: Follow the manual’s number rules for duration
rules.statement: Use fractions written in words if users only need a general idea of values.
rules.body_excerpt:
- There are 7 minutes and 30 seconds remaining. [Numerals for 2 and above]
- The hearing adjourned for 2 hours. [Numerals for 2 and above]
- The committee will break for lunch for one hour. [Words for zero and one]
- Although we allowed candidates 1 minute to answer each question, most took over 2 minutes. [Numerals when comparing duration]
- I noted faults at these time stamps: 0 minutes 45 seconds, 1 minute 4 seconds and 3 minutes 8 seconds. [Numerals for a series of numbers showing duration]

Use fractions written in words if users only need a general idea of values.

Only use decimal numbers if they are the best way to explain what people need to know. But be aware that some people might not understand the decimal’s time value. For example, 1.25 hours is 1 hour 15 minutes, not 1 hour 25 minutes.

It is usually better to avoid decimals and include the number and unit of time.
rules.violation_condition: A duration intended to give only a general idea of its value uses a numerical fraction rather than a fraction written in words.
context_preconditions: Applies to duration fractions where users need only a general idea.
Does not require every duration to be converted into a fraction.

heading_path: Use the correct term when referring to diplomats
Emails and letters to ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios
rules.statement: Conclude with 'Yours faithfully'.
rules.body_excerpt:
In formal correspondence with ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios:

- Open with ‘Your Excellency’.
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

In informal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Dear High Commissioner’ or ‘Dear Ambassador’.
- Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.
rules.violation_condition: Formal correspondence to an ambassador, high commissioner or nuncio does not conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.
context_preconditions: Applies to emails and letters to ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios.
Formal correspondence concludes with ‘Yours faithfully’.
The informal close, ‘Yours sincerely’, is bd6dcc3a42cbab05's rule.

heading_path: Check the correct name of an organisation
rules.statement: Spell out the shortened form the first time, unless the organisation's name is known only by the shortened form.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the organisation’s shortened form only if the organisation regularly uses it in its own content.

For example, the Department of Home Affairs uses ‘Home Affairs’ as the shortened form. It would be inappropriate to use ‘DHA’ to refer to Home Affairs. However, Defence Housing Australia does use the initialism ‘DHA’, so using it to refer to that organisation would be appropriate.

Spell out the shortened form the first time, unless the organisation’s name is known only by the shortened form.
rules.violation_condition: A first mention uses only an unexpanded shortened or incomplete name when the full title is required, or expands a name known only by its shortened form.
context_preconditions: Assess the first mention of the organisation or introduction of its shortened form.
Use the full title on first mention in a publication, including legal-name words or their official shortened forms.
For an organisation known only by its shortened form, retain that form rather than spelling it out, as the IKEA contrast demonstrates.
On subsequent mentions in print documents, words such as ‘proprietary’ and ‘limited’ and their corresponding shortened forms may be omitted.
compliant_examples: Zoning laws allowed IKEA to lease the land.
Defence Housing Australia (DHA) provides housing for Defence members and their families. DHA also provides other related services.
violating_examples: DHA provides housing for Defence members and their families.
Zoning laws allowed Ingvar Kamprad Elmtaryd Agunnaryd (IKEA) to lease the land.

heading_path: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma
Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
rules.statement: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
rules.body_excerpt: Use commas after [adverbial phrases](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/127) and [adverbial clauses](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/127). Adverbs – such as ‘first’ and ‘during’ – modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
rules.violation_condition: An adverbial phrase or clause that opens a sentence, including a conditional clause beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’, is not followed by a comma.
context_preconditions: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses, including conditional clauses.
compliant_examples: Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour. [Adverbial clause]
During the meeting, we discussed item 9. [Adverbial phrase]
Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time. [A conditional adverbial clause]

heading_path: Focus on the person, not the disability
rules.statement: Mention disability only when it's relevant to the content.
rules.body_excerpt:
Mention disability only when it’s relevant to the content.

When you are writing about people with disability, focus on the person. Engage with people through [user research](https://www.dta.gov.au/help-and-advice/build-and-improve-services/user-research).

User research can uncover whether an individual or community preference is:

- person-first language
- identity-first language.

Use person-first language for Australian Government content, unless user research says otherwise.
rules.violation_condition: A person's disability is mentioned even though it is irrelevant to the content.
context_preconditions: Applies when deciding whether to mention disability at all.

heading_path: Don’t use exclamation marks in general
rules.statement: Use them sparingly in less formal content such as promotional material and social media posts.
rules.body_excerpt:
- That can’t be true!
- Stand at ease!

Use them sparingly in less formal content such as promotional material and social media posts. Be aware that exclamation marks can create a sense of panic or stress.
rules.violation_condition: In less formal content, exclamation marks are used often, or are used where they can create a sense of panic or stress, such as in an emergency message.
context_preconditions: Applies to less formal government content, including promotional material and social media posts.
Formal content is subject to the separate restriction on using exclamation marks at all.
compliant_examples: Congratulations to our 2020 Australia Day Award recipients!
Happy international mother language day! #ourAPS believes in the importance of cultural and linguistic diversity (CALD) for a sustainable and harmonious Australian society.
violating_examples: A state of emergency has been declared for all areas of the ACT!

heading_path: Put a non-breaking space between the chunks of digits
rules.statement: Put a non-breaking space between the chunks of digits
rules.body_excerpt:
Use a non-breaking space between chunks of digits in a telephone number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up the number. The telephone number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity   to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.
rules.violation_condition: The separator between displayed telephone-number chunks is a breaking space or another separator instead of a non-breaking space; in print, it is not a narrow no-break space.
context_preconditions: Applies between chunks of a displayed telephone number, not inside its tel: URL.
Use a non-breaking space, U+00A0, in the general case.
For print, use a narrow no-break space, U+202F.
In HTML,   represents the general non-breaking space.

heading_path: Put paragraphs in the order that makes sense to the user
rules.statement: Put paragraphs in the order that makes sense to the user
rules.body_excerpt:
Order paragraphs in a logical sequence, such as:

- steps in a transaction
- the order of importance
- cause then effect
- problem then solution
- pros then cons.

This helps people follow related ideas or [steps in a sequence](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/78).

Arrange paragraphs under brief, meaningful [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/structuring-content/headings). Headings help users understand what the paragraphs cover.
rules.violation_condition: Paragraphs occur in an order that makes the intended task, argument or sequence difficult to follow.
context_preconditions: Appropriate sequences include transaction steps, importance, cause then effect, problem then solution, and pros then cons.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames
rules.statement: Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Oodgeroo Noonuccal
- Clive James
- Minjee Lee
- Miles Franklin
- Fiona Katauskas
- Beatie Bow
- King O’Malley

Capitalise the initials of people’s given names. Write them unspaced and without full stops. Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.
rules.violation_condition: The space joining given-name initials to the family name allows a line break.
context_preconditions: Applies at the boundary between given-name initials and a family name.

heading_path: Requirements and standards for video and audio
Include subtitles or captions for video
Time the captions and subtitles to match the dialogue
rules.statement: Keep captions and subtitles short: no more than 2 lines, with no more than 42 characters per line.
rules.body_excerpt:
Keep captions and subtitles short: no more than 2 lines, with no more than 42 characters per line. Make line breaks where there is a natural break in the sentence (for example, after a comma).

People read about 2 lines of text in 2 seconds. Test that users can read the captions in the time available.

Don’t leave the captions on the screen:

- after the speech has finished
- across the transition from one scene to the next.

Try to ensure a small break of at least 4 frames between subtitles.

Review and edit the accuracy and synchronised timing of the captions for pre recorded video.
rules.violation_condition: A caption or subtitle has more than 2 lines, or a line contains more than 42 characters.
context_preconditions: The text is a caption or subtitle block.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
Use consistent formatting and punctuation for captions and titles
rules.statement: Don't use a full stop to end the title or caption, even if it is a complete sentence.
rules.body_excerpt:
Align captions and titles to the left. Place captions for decorative images, such as photographs, below the image.

Titles and captions don’t need to be a complete sentence. Other grammar and punctuation rules for titles and captions are:

- Capitalise the first word and proper nouns only.
- Don’t use a full stop to end the title or caption, even if it is a complete sentence.

All titles and captions should have the same:

- structure (parallel structure)
- terms and shortened forms as those used in the rest of the content (such as [acronyms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/190))
- font and typeface.
rules.violation_condition: An image title or caption ends with a full stop.
context_preconditions: Applies even when the title or caption is a complete sentence.
This concerns the ending, not the permitted full stop after a figure number in some organisational styles.

heading_path: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals
rules.statement: Use numerals, not words, for centuries.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use numerals, not words, for centuries. This is an exception to the rule for [ordinal numbers](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/ordinal-numbers#use_words_for_ordinals_up_to_ninth_and_numerals_for_10th_and_above).

Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.

Don’t use shortened forms, such as 18C or C18, unless you have limited space.

Don’t use superscript for the ordinal suffix.
rules.violation_condition: A century number is spelled out in words rather than written as an ordinal numeral.
context_preconditions: Also applies in adjectival compounds such as ‘19th-century’.
compliant_examples: the 18th century
a 19th-century writer
violating_examples: a nineteenth-century writer
the eighteenth century

heading_path: Include all parts of the periodical
rules.statement: Include all parts of the periodical
rules.body_excerpt:
Periodicals get published at regular times. Each issue of a periodical is complete but also part of a set or volume. Most periodicals are online. Some no longer have a print version.

Because each issue is complete in itself, you must include the following:

- title
- year, volume and issue number
- name of the sponsoring body
- name of the publisher or distributor or both
- copyright details
- restrictions on circulation
- International Standard Serial Number (ISSN).
rules.violation_condition: An issue of a periodical is missing its title, year, volume or issue number, sponsoring body, publisher or distributor, copyright details, circulation restrictions or ISSN.
context_preconditions: Applies to each issue of a periodical.

heading_path: Repeat words instead of using a hanging hyphen
rules.statement: Repeat words instead of using a hanging hyphen
rules.body_excerpt: Hanging (or floating) hyphens connect 2 words to a base word or a number that they share.
rules.violation_condition: A coordinated expression uses a hanging hyphen to omit a repeated base word or number.
context_preconditions: Coordinated words or prefixes share a base word or number.
Repeating the shared material is preferred over a hanging hyphen.
The hanging forms are presented as grammatical examples of the construction, not as incorrect English.
compliant_examples: full-time and part-time positions

heading_path: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Style for First Australian languages needs to recognise continuing cultures
rules.statement: Never refer to them as 'extinct'.
rules.body_excerpt: Hundreds of distinct First Nations languages and dialects are alive and spoken today. Never refer to them as ‘extinct’. Many communities are working to revive their languages. The preferred term to describe these languages is ‘sleeping’.
rules.violation_condition: A First Nations language is described as ‘extinct’.
context_preconditions: Apply to First Nations languages.
For languages being revived, the preferred description is ‘sleeping’.

heading_path: Use the standard units of measurement
rules.statement: don't place a full stop after a unit of measurement.
rules.body_excerpt:
Australia uses the metric system for most quantities:

- The modern form of the metric system is the [International System of Units](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units/) (SI).
- Australia also uses some non-SI legal units of measurement, which are listed in [Schedules 1 and 2 of the National Measurement Regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Details/F2012C00400).

The National Measurement Institute oversees [Australian units of measurement](https://www.industry.gov.au/regulations-and-standards/australias-measurement-system). The governing legislation is the [*National Measurement Act 1960*](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C1960A00064).

Don’t use the non-SI legal units of measurement for international content. The exception is when you have checked that users will understand and accept them.

Rules for units of measurement:

- Punctuation: don’t place a full stop after a unit of measurement.
- Capitalisation: use capitals only if the unit represents a proper name.
- Plural and possessive: units don’t have a plural or possessive form.
- Start of a sentence: write out the unit in full.
- Spacing: use a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.
rules.violation_condition: A unit symbol has a full stop added as abbreviation punctuation.
context_preconditions: Applies to unit symbols.
Do not flag ordinary sentence-ending punctuation.

heading_path: Space en dashes in sentences to set off non-essential information
rules.statement: If you remove the content between the en dashes, the rest of the sentence must be a complete sentence.
rules.body_excerpt:
There was no time to plan – a shortcoming that would later cost millions.

Make sure the rest of the sentence makes sense.

If you remove the content between the en dashes, the rest of the sentence must be a complete sentence.
rules.violation_condition: Removing the parenthetical material enclosed by en dashes leaves an incomplete sentence, or neither side of a single punctuating en dash is a complete sentence.
context_preconditions: With paired en dashes, test the sentence remaining after the enclosed content is removed.
With one en dash, at least one side must be a complete sentence.
compliant_examples: There was no time to plan – a shortcoming that would later cost millions.
The allies – the USA, Australia and New Zealand – signed the pact in 1951.
Solar, wind, hydro and tidal power – all are viable options for renewable energy.
violating_examples: Solar, wind, hydro and tidal power – are viable options for renewable energy.

heading_path: Write certain prefixes with a hyphen
rules.statement: All words formed with 'ex-', meaning 'former', are hyphenated.
rules.body_excerpt:
Regardless of whether the rest of the word starts with a vowel:

- Many words with the prefix ‘co-’, meaning ‘joint’, have hyphens after the ‘co’.
- All words formed with ‘ex-’, meaning ‘former’, are hyphenated.
rules.violation_condition: The prefix ex meaning former is attached to its base without a hyphen.
context_preconditions: Ex means former.
The requirement applies whether the base starts with a vowel or a consonant.
compliant_examples: ex-councillor, ex-president

heading_path: Write all numbers as numerals in these specific situations
rules.statement: numerals only
rules.body_excerpt:
Use well-understood conventions to write [mathematical relationships](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/145). Keep relationships together so they are easily understood. To do this use:

- numerals only
- the correct operator characters
- spacing between numerals and operators
- non-breaking spaces.
rules.violation_condition: A number in a mathematical relationship, such as an equation or ratio, is written as a word.
context_preconditions: Applies to numerical terms in mathematical relationships, including equations and ratios.
compliant_examples: a ratio of 7∶1

heading_path: Follow normal punctuation rules for content in brackets
rules.statement: If the content inside the brackets is a full sentence, include the end punctuation inside the brackets.
rules.body_excerpt:
The winning tenderer (a local company), signed the contract on Tuesday.

If the content inside the brackets is a full sentence, include the end punctuation inside the brackets.
rules.violation_condition: A complete bracketed sentence lacks its end punctuation before the closing bracket.
context_preconditions: The bracketed content is a full sentence.
A complete bracketed sentence must not be embedded inside another sentence.
compliant_examples: The department was in a heritage-listed building. (The building was designed by award-winning architect Enrico Taglietti.)

heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for the formal titles of current members of parliament.
rules.body_excerpt:
Senator Lines is the Deputy President and Chair of Committees in the 46th Parliament.

Use initial capitals for the formal titles of current members of parliament.
rules.violation_condition: the formal title of a current member of parliament written in lower case, or parliamentary terms that are not formal titles capitalised
context_preconditions: Use lower case for parliamentary terms that are not formal titles (e.g. member of parliament, senator, frontbench, backbencher, crossbencher).
compliant_examples: They met with Senator Griff.
Senator Pauline Hanson
He was a former senator for Tasmania, serving from 1947 to 1951.
Mr Adam Bandt MP
She moved from the backbench to take the new ministerial portfolio.

rules.statement: If there's any doubt, define the abbreviation on first use.
rules.body_excerpt:
Thank you for your email about errors in the third para of the webpage *How to apply for a special use permit*.

Abbreviations are useful in very limited circumstances:

- in a table or chart, where space is unavailable for the full form of the word – provide a note under the table or chart giving the full form
- when using ‘cont’ to show continuing text in another part of content (for example, on another page of a print newsletter) – the full form of the word is more helpful where space allows.

Semi-formal and informal content uses abbreviations more often. Use abbreviations only if users will understand what they mean. If there’s any doubt, define the abbreviation on first use.

Avoid using abbreviations in any public-facing content.
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviation whose meaning may be unfamiliar to the intended users appears without a definition at its first use.
context_preconditions: Applies when there is doubt that users will understand an abbreviation.

heading_path: Avoid using square brackets in parentheses
rules.statement: Avoid using square brackets in parentheses
rules.body_excerpt: Reword the text to avoid square brackets inside of parentheses wherever possible.
rules.violation_condition: Square brackets are nested inside parentheses where the information could reasonably be presented without nested brackets.
context_preconditions: Avoid this nesting wherever possible.
Square brackets remain the prescribed inner brackets when parenthetical information must be placed inside parentheses.
compliant_examples: Australia’s Parliament House opened on 9 May 1988. The architects were Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp (New York).

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: Don't use 'Executive summary'.
rules.body_excerpt:
For long reports, use a summary to present findings, recommendations and conclusions.

- Name the summary to show its purpose. For example, you can use ‘Recommendations’ or ‘Summary’*.*
- Don't use ‘Executive summary’. Although this is common, it is not best practice.
rules.violation_condition: the phrase 'Executive summary' used as a heading

heading_path: Write certain prefixes with a hyphen
rules.statement: Hyphens link a prefix to a word that starts with a capital letter.
rules.body_excerpt: Hyphens link a prefix to a word that starts with a capital letter.
rules.violation_condition: A prefix is attached to a capital-initial base without a linking hyphen.
context_preconditions: The capital letter starts the base word, not merely the whole expression at the start of a sentence.
compliant_examples: pro-European
un-Australian activities

heading_path: Write all numbers as numerals in these specific situations
rules.statement: Lists or blocks of data must consist of numerals, or people will find them hard to understand.
rules.body_excerpt:
Lists or blocks of data must consist of numerals, or people will find them hard to understand. Always use numerals in graphs, charts and [tables](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/45). Numerals save space and help people scan, find and compare values quickly.

Restrict data to key indicators and results. Keep the presentation of data as simple as possible, and use consistent units and magnitudes.
rules.violation_condition: Numerical values in a data list, data block, graph, chart or table are written as words.
context_preconditions: Applies to numerical data, not to non-numerical labels or explanatory text.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
rules.statement: use a colon after the number to separate it from the title text
rules.body_excerpt:
Many publications refer to all images as ‘figures’. Complex publications with many images can use different categories (such as figures, maps or photographs).

In long-form content, number titles that go with images using ‘figure labels’. You don’t need to number images in a brochure, an infographic or a simple, stand-alone page with only a few images.

The purpose of numbering images is to help people find a specific image. Put the number before the main text of the image title.

To number an image title in a long document:

- Use the ‘Insert caption’ function in applications to create a label.
- Select the ‘Figure’ label option, and the option to position the label above the image.
- Do not select the ‘Exclude label from caption’ box.

The labels will convert to titles that are automatically numbered and styled for you. Check that you:

- start the numbering at the beginning of the document
- use a colon after the number to separate it from the title text
- use an initial capital for title text that comes after the colon.

Some disciplines use a full stop after the number. If your organisation uses this style, apply it consistently.

Use the ‘Cross-reference’ function to insert t
rules.violation_condition: A numbered image title lacks a colon between its number and title text, unless it consistently follows an organisational full-stop style.
context_preconditions: Applies to numbered image titles.
A full stop after the number is acceptable if the organisation uses that style consistently.

heading_path: Write certain prefixes with a hyphen
rules.statement: Don't use hyphens if the 2 words end and start with different vowels.
rules.body_excerpt: Don’t use hyphens if the 2 words end and start with different vowels. The combined word doesn’t place the same vowel together.
rules.violation_condition: A prefix and base meeting at different vowels have an unnecessary hyphen, or lack the exception's separating hyphen when the base has a single syllable.
context_preconditions: A vowel-final prefix meets a base beginning with a different vowel.
A single-syllable vowel-initial base takes a separating hyphen.
Two-syllable prefixes are covered by their more specific rule.
Capital-initial, numerical and italic bases follow their specific prefix rules.
compliant_examples: reallocate
prearrange
de-ice
triennial

heading_path: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives
Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
rules.statement: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
rules.body_excerpt:
Use commas between items in a sentence list. Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.

This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: Items in a sentence list are not separated by commas, apart from the last 2, which are joined by ‘and’ or ‘or’.
context_preconditions: Sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.
compliant_examples: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.
The consultation involved businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits.
The applicant was willing to learn, eager to work and well prepared.

heading_path: Choose between a decimal value or fraction
rules.statement: In text, write decimal values as numerals.
rules.body_excerpt:
You can express a less-than-whole number as a decimal or as a fraction.

In text, write [decimal values as numerals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/198#write_all_numbers_as_numerals_in_these_specific_situations). Write [fractions as words](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/198#use_words_for_2_and_above_in_these_specific_situations).
rules.violation_condition: A decimal value in text is written in words rather than numerals.
context_preconditions: In text.

heading_path: Set off most foreign words and phrases
rules.statement: Foreign words and phrases should generally be avoided in government writing, unless there is no English equivalent.
rules.body_excerpt: Italics contrast words and phrases that are not in English from surrounding text. Foreign words and phrases should generally be avoided in government writing, unless there is no English equivalent.
rules.violation_condition: A foreign word or phrase is used where an English equivalent is available.
context_preconditions: An English equivalent is available.
Words absorbed into Standard Australian English are not treated as foreign expressions.
First Nations languages are Australian languages, not foreign languages.

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: should be in the main part of the report if people will need the content to understand the report – for example, if the introduction includes terms of reference
rules.body_excerpt:
A report often has a foreword, preface or introduction. They have different functions and you would rarely need them all.

A foreword:

- is always in the preliminary content
- is usually written by someone other than the author and often includes their signature
- explains the purpose of the report and why it’s important
- helps a wider audience to relate to the report.

A preface:

- is always in the preliminary content
- can replace a short introduction
- is written by the author and can include the author's signature
- tells the user why and how the report was prepared
- can include a short list of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it's a new version or update.

An introduction:

- can be in the preliminary content or main part of the report
- should be in the main part of the report if people will need the content to understand the report – for example, if the introduction includes terms of reference
- is by the author or someone else
- does not include a signature
- can replace a preface to discuss why and how the report was prepared
- includes long lists of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it’s a new version or update.
rules.violation_condition: An introduction containing material essential to understanding the report is placed in preliminary content rather than the main body.
context_preconditions: The introduction contains material readers need to understand the report, such as terms of reference.
Otherwise, the introduction may be in the preliminary content or the main body.

heading_path: Refer to the table in the text
rules.statement: Don't repeat the whole title of the table in the text.
rules.body_excerpt:
Tables support the discussion in the text, not the other way around. It is essential to refer to a table in the text.

A single table on a webpage does not need a table number. If you use tables repeatedly, number tables and include the table number when you refer to the table in the text.

When using a table:

- Place the table close to where you mention it in the text and after the paragraph that refers to it. In print, the table should be on the same or facing page.
- Ensure that the table number referenced in the text matches the table number in the title.
- Don’t repeat the whole title of the table in the text.
- Don’t refer to ‘the table below’ or ‘the table above’.
- Ensure that the information in the text is consistent with the information in the table.

Your text comments on or interprets the table. Where possible, avoid repeating the text or data in the table word for word.
rules.violation_condition: Body text repeats the table’s complete title when referring to it.
compliant_examples: Table 2 shows that average rainfall has …
violating_examples: Table 2 (Average monthly rainfall, June 2017 to December 2019) shows that average rainfall has …

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: does not include a signature
rules.body_excerpt:
A report often has a foreword, preface or introduction. They have different functions and you would rarely need them all.

A foreword:

- is always in the preliminary content
- is usually written by someone other than the author and often includes their signature
- explains the purpose of the report and why it’s important
- helps a wider audience to relate to the report.

A preface:

- is always in the preliminary content
- can replace a short introduction
- is written by the author and can include the author's signature
- tells the user why and how the report was prepared
- can include a short list of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it's a new version or update.

An introduction:

- can be in the preliminary content or main part of the report
- should be in the main part of the report if people will need the content to understand the report – for example, if the introduction includes terms of reference
- is by the author or someone else
- does not include a signature
- can replace a preface to discuss why and how the report was prepared
- includes long lists of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it’s a new version or update.
rules.violation_condition: The report's introduction includes a signature.
context_preconditions: The content is the report's introduction.

heading_path: Follow the guidance on capitals for titles and government terms
rules.statement: In these cases, use the form of the name as it is written in the legislation.
rules.body_excerpt:
The Senior Policy Adviser offered their view ...

Follow the rules of [capitalisation for government terms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/136), for example:

- government programs and agreements
- mentions of parliament
- references to states and territories.

Legal material has its own conventions for capitalisation. Content that has a legislative focus might use complementary sources to the [guidance on citing legal material in this manual](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/163).

Legal documents often use initial capitals to show terms with a defined meaning (such as ‘Department’, ‘Schedule’, ‘Vendor’ and ‘Recipient’). In these cases, use the form of the name as it is written in the legislation.
rules.violation_condition: A legislatively defined name or term is written in a form that differs from its form in the legislation.
context_preconditions: Legal content uses a legislatively defined name or term whose initial capitals signal its defined meaning.

heading_path: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Strengths-based language respects continuous cultures and connections
rules.statement: Use empowering, strengths-based language.
rules.body_excerpt:
Content about First Nations people has often focused on ‘problems’. This has 2 outcomes: making First Australians ‘the problem’ or continuing a deficit discourse. Neither is acceptable.

It’s important to acknowledge the many wrongs and ongoing injustices that stem from our shared history. And it's not about ignoring issues. But it is just as important to acknowledge the strength of those First Australians whose cultures survive and thrive today.

Make sure to:

- Use empowering, strengths-based language.
- Tell positive stories.
- Emphasise ongoing connections to community, culture and country.
rules.violation_condition: Language frames First Nations people themselves as problems or deficits, rather than recognising their agency and strengths.
context_preconditions: Discussion of wrongs, ongoing injustices and other issues remains appropriate.
Flag deficit framing rather than merely the presence of negative facts.
compliant_examples: The program supports First Nations people to achieve their goals.
violating_examples: The program seeks to address the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander problems within the community.

rules.statement: Eliminate unnecessary words
rules.body_excerpt:
Make each word work for its place in the sentence. Sentence structure is clearer if each word plays a necessary role. Clear sentences improve readability.

It helps to test the combination to know which words are necessary.

Keep the words that play a critical function in the sentence. Remove all the words except the [subject, verb and object (if applicable)](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/120#a_full_sentence_is_grammatically_complete).

Check if the sentence is grammatically correct when you remove the other words.

Build the sentence back together, leaving out any words that aren’t absolutely necessary. Adverbs and adjectives are usually good candidates to leave out in this kind of test.

Check if the basic meaning of the sentence remains, and if it’s grammatical. Then check if the words you’ve removed are really working to keep their place.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence contains dispensable wording that adds no necessary meaning, including semantically empty ‘there is’ or ‘there are’ constructions.
context_preconditions: Retain words needed to make the meaning clear.
Flag ‘there is’ and ‘there are’ only when they add words without adding meaning.
compliant_examples: If anything doesn’t fit within this framework ...
Call us if you have any questions.
We provide statistics for trade reports. Contact us with trade data requests and we’ll respond within 2 business days.
violating_examples: If you were unsure about any of the information or needed more details, you are welcome to telephone our office to acquire what you needed.

Our team will happily provide you with any statistics you might be seeking for the purpose of producing better and more factually accurate trade reports. Let us know if you’re seeking specific trade data and we’ll seek to provide it to you as soon as we can, usually within 2 business days.
If there is anything that doesn’t fit within this framework ...

heading_path: Keep hyphens and all parts of compound family names
rules.statement: Write all parts of compound family names.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Kath Day-Knight
- Alen-Igor O’Hran

Write all parts of compound family names. Keep the compound when writing a person’s family name.
rules.violation_condition: A reference to a person's compound family name omits one or more parts of that compound.
context_preconditions: Applies to compound family names, including when the given name is omitted.
A person with more than one family name who is known by only one is not a compound family name; that is the multiple-family-names rule.
compliant_examples: William Delafield Cook

heading_path: Use the appropriate form for members of state and territory parliaments
Address certain office holders in state and NT parliaments as ‘Honourable’

rules.body_excerpt:
- NSW: The Hon Benjamin Cameron Franklin MLC, President of the Legislative Council
- NT: The Hon Robyn Lambley MLA, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
- Qld: The Hon John-Paul Langbroek MP, Minister for Education and the Arts [Serving minister]
- SA: The Hon Jing Shyuan Lee MLC [Member of the Legislative Council]
- Tas: The Hon Joshua Willie MP, Leader of the Opposition

- WA: The Hon Maryka Groenewald MLC [Member of the Legislative Council]

Office holders in the ACT Legislative Assembly don’t use the title ‘Honourable’. Ministers in theACT have more than one portfolio. Address emails and letters to them using the ministerial title appropriate to the topic.
rules.violation_condition: An ACT Legislative Assembly office holder is addressed as ‘Honourable’ or ‘Hon’ by virtue of that ACT office.

heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for possessive names
rules.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for possessive names
rules.body_excerpt:
Don’t use an apostrophe for topographic terms involving possessives. Official place names are not possessive and do not usually include punctuation.

Refer to related [guidance on Australian place names](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/134#check_official_place_names_and_style_them_correctly).
rules.violation_condition: A topographic name contains an apostrophe inserted to mark an apparent possessive.
context_preconditions: Applies to possessive-looking elements within topographic names.
The explanatory statement that place names do not usually include punctuation is not a blanket prohibition on every punctuation mark.
compliant_examples: Careys Peak
violating_examples: Carey’s Peak

heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
rules.statement: The division slash is unspaced.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the division symbol (÷) or the division slash ( ∕ ). People sometimes use the forward slash (/) to show division as well.

Use [non-breaking spaces](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/mathematical-relationships#use_a_nonbreaking_space_to_keep_characters_and_symbols_together) around the division symbol.

Programming languages and Excel use the forward slash (/) for division.

In most cases, it's best to use the division symbol (÷). The division slash is easily confused with the forward slash which is also used to show alternatives.

In Unicode, the symbol for division is U+00F7 and the division slash is U+2215.

However, division slashes might appear in expressions you have to reproduce in your content – for example, in algebraic fractions.

The division slash is unspaced. This is a style convention in mathematics. But consider adding a narrow no-break space around the division slash to make the expression clearer. You can also use a thin space, but it will break across lines.

The Unicode characters are:

- division symbol – U+00F7
- division slash – U+2215
- narrow no-break space – U+202F
- thin space – U+2009.
rules.violation_condition: A division slash has surrounding whitespace other than the specifically permitted narrow no-break or thin spaces used for clarity.
context_preconditions: Applies to the division slash ∕, U+2215.
No surrounding spaces are the default.
Narrow no-break spaces, U+202F, or thin spaces, U+2009, may surround the slash to improve clarity.

rules.statement: Limit the use of abbreviations
rules.body_excerpt: Abbreviations contain the first single letter or first few letters of a word. They don’t include the last letter of a word.
rules.violation_condition: An avoidable abbreviation appears in general or public-facing content rather than its full form, outside the limited uses the page allows.
context_preconditions: Applies to general content where using the full word is possible, and to public-facing content.
Abbreviations are permitted in tables or charts where there is insufficient space for the full word; the full-form note is checked separately.
‘cont’ may mark text continuing elsewhere, but the full word is preferred where space allows.
The page recognises more frequent abbreviation use in semi-formal and informal content; the audience-understanding requirement still applies.
compliant_examples: Thank you for your email about errors in the third paragraph of the webpage How to apply for a special use permit.
violating_examples: Thank you for your email about errors in the third para of the webpage How to apply for a special use permit.

heading_path: Choose between numerals or words for currency
rules.statement: Use numerals and symbols for amounts of money.
rules.body_excerpt: Use numerals and symbols for amounts of [money](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/currency).
rules.violation_condition: A monetary amount uses words instead of the numeral-and-currency-symbol form, outside the permitted approximations and figures of speech.
context_preconditions: Applies to monetary amounts, including zero and one.
Money may be written entirely in words for approximations and figures of speech.
Large rounded monetary amounts may combine numerals, currency symbols and scale words.
compliant_examples: They self-declared a $0 turnover.
The government’s new policy will save thousands of dollars.
That’s my two cents worth.

heading_path: Use tables if they make content easier to read
rules.statement: a title (also called a caption)
rules.body_excerpt:
User needs:

- I can change the content without losing information or structure.
- I can find and navigate the content and determine where I am on the webpage.

Fundamentals:

- Tables can be made accessible for all users. The World Wide Web Consortium has [tips for setting up tables](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/tips/).
- You must give a table:
- a title (also called a [caption](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49))
- row and column headings
- information (entries)
- a cross-reference in the text.
- You may also need to add notes below the table to help users understand the information and where it comes from.
- Don’t rely on colour as the only visual means of conveying information in tables.
- Don’t leave cells empty. Use ‘zero’ or ‘nil’ or 'n/a' where there is no data. If it is numeric data, use the numeric zero (0). Only use zero if that is the true value.

WCAG quick reference:

- [1.3.1 Info and relationships – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#info-and-relationships)
- [1.4.1 Use of color – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#use-of-color)
rules.violation_condition: A table has no title or caption.

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: Wherever it features, people should be able to easily find copyright and other information about the report.
rules.body_excerpt:
There are many items you can include in preliminary content. Some are best suited to printed publications. Judge what you need for your report.

Australian Government reports published online should include the same information as a printed version.

A title page should include the following:

- title
- subtitle, if any
- author’s name
- name of the sponsor, if applicable.

It can also have additional details such as the name of a compiler, translator, reviser or illustrator.

The reverse title page, or ‘imprint’ page, includes details that don’t appear on the title page, such as:

- copyright notices, including copyright held by others such as photographers and illustrators
- the publisher’s imprint or name and address
- lists of editions and reprints
- list of other volumes in a multi-volume set (this can also be on a separate page)
- identifying numbers and library classification data
- name of others contributing to the document, such as the editor, designer or illustrator.

Many online reports put imprint page material on the splash screen or landing page. Wherever it features, people should be able to easily find copyright and other information about the report.
rules.violation_condition: Copyright and other imprint information is absent or located or labelled so that readers cannot readily find it.
context_preconditions: Copyright and other imprint information may appear on a reverse title page, landing page, splash screen or another suitable location.
In print, the inside front cover or back cover can carry reverse-title-page information.

heading_path: Stress words with special emphasis, but rarely
rules.statement: If you do this, write 'emphasis added' in square brackets following the italicised text.
rules.body_excerpt: Sometimes, you might want to add italics to quotations to bring attention to particular words or phrases. If you do this, write ‘emphasis added’ in square brackets following the italicised text. This way, people will know the italics didn’t appear in the original quotation.
rules.violation_condition: Italic emphasis in a quotation lacks the appropriate square-bracketed provenance label, uses the wrong label for its source, or places the label before rather than after the required text.
context_preconditions: A quotation contains italic emphasis.
Added emphasis is identified by ‘emphasis added’ in square brackets following the italicised text.
Emphasis retained from the original is identified by ‘emphasis from original’ in square brackets following the quotation.
Determining whether the provenance label is accurate requires access to the original quotation.
compliant_examples: ‘Subsequently, in 1903, Parliament passed a unanimous resolution that it should be flown.’ [emphasis added]

rules.statement: Number the questions
rules.body_excerpt:
For forms that have more than one question, number the questions.

This is helpful for the user if they need to leave the form and return to it later. It can also make it easier for them to get help to fill it in, and for them to work across a paper and digital version.
rules.violation_condition: A form containing more than one question leaves its questions unnumbered.
context_preconditions: Applies to forms with more than one question.

heading_path: Plan blog posts with a specific purpose and structure
rules.statement: Include a call to action at the end of your post.
rules.body_excerpt:
Include a call to action at the end of your post. Examples of calls to action include invitations to:

- take the next step in using the service or product
- give feedback
- get emails about new posts or news items
- subscribe to a newsletter
- get more detailed information on a topic
- respond to a survey.
rules.violation_condition: A blog post does not end with a call to action.
context_preconditions: Applies to blog posts.
The listed types of invitation are examples, not a requirement to include every type.
compliant_examples: To bookmark the topics you find most useful, visit the Style Manual.

heading_path: Address certain office holders of the Australian Parliament as ‘Honourable’
rules.statement: The abbreviation for 'Honourable' is 'Hon' without a full stop.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the title ‘Honourable’ for ministers (including the prime minister) and parliamentary secretaries in the Australian Parliament. The title is given to these office holders because they are members of the [Federal Executive Council](https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/House_of_Representatives/Powers_practice_and_procedure/Practice7/HTML/Chapter2/Federal_Executive_Council). They retain the title for life.

The abbreviation for ‘Honourable’ is ‘Hon’ without a full stop.
rules.violation_condition: One of the specified official titles is abbreviated using an incorrect short form or a full stop, such as ‘Hon.’, ‘Rt. Hon.’, ‘Pres.’, ‘Ald.’ or ‘Cr.’.
context_preconditions: The specified abbreviations are Hon for Honourable, Rt Hon for Right Honourable, Pres for President, Ald for Alderman and Cr for Councillor.
The permission to use Rt Hon is stated for emails and letters to lord mayors.
This rule checks an abbreviation when used; it does not require replacing a full title with an abbreviation.
The separate preference for President over Pres still applies.

heading_path: Requirements and standards for video and audio
Include subtitles or captions for video
rules.statement: Use Australian terms and spelling for an Australian audience, regardless of the accent or intention of the speaker.
rules.body_excerpt:
User needs:

I can access equivalent information to anything contained in a video or audio file.

Web Content Accessibility Guidelines success criteria:

- [1.2.2 Captions (prerecorded) – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#captions-prerecorded)
- [1.2.4 Captions (live) – level AA](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#captions-live)

Open captions, which the user cannot turn off, are burned onto the video itself. Closed captions can be turned on or off by the user.

If you have a choice, closed captions are preferable to subtitles or open captions. Some media players also allow for multilingual captions that users can select on demand if they need translations.

Use Australian terms and spelling for an Australian audience, regardless of the accent or intention of the speaker. Government agencies might use alternative spellings in video content for some overseas audiences.

Closed captions come in many file formats. SRT is a common format and is compatible with most online platforms and media players.

Load the closed caption file onto the video platform as a separate file to the video file. This allows the user to turn the captions on or off.

You can edit closed ca
rules.violation_condition: Captions or subtitles intended for an Australian audience use non-Australian terms or spelling merely to reproduce the speaker’s accent or intended spelling.
