context_preconditions: The text is captions or subtitles for an Australian audience.
Alternative spellings may be used in government video content for some overseas audiences.

heading_path: Combine numerals and words for dates in body text
rules.statement: For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month.
rules.body_excerpt:
In Australia, the conventional sequence for dates is ‘day month year’. Use this sequence when expressing dates in numerals and words.

For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month. Don’t include a comma or any other punctuation.

Spell out the name of the day if it is being used, but don’t include a comma after the day.

The names of months and days start with an initial capital because they are [proper nouns](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/types-words/nouns#proper_nouns_are_the_names_of_people_and_specific_things”).
rules.violation_condition: An ordinary body-text date has a day or year written in words, an abbreviated month or weekday, or an entirely numeric presentation outside a space-limited context.
context_preconditions: Use the words-and-numerals form in ordinary content.
Spell out a weekday when it is included.
Spell out the month when the day or year is omitted.
Abbreviated words and numeric dates are allowed when space is limited, including in tables.
Separate conventions apply to data systems and international interchange.
The day-only ordinal exception is handled by the ordinal-date rule.
compliant_examples: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Saturday 22 December.
31 December 2020
Thursday 31 December 2020
violating_examples: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Sat 22 Dec.

heading_path: Design headings and other elements to help the user scan the page
rules.statement: Start with the most important idea first.
rules.body_excerpt:
Once you have decided on the type of structure you need to use, plan the structural elements.

- Use a logical hierarchy or sequential steps for [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/51).
- Write a topic sentence for each [paragraph](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/53).
- Display important information in [lists](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/56), [callout boxes](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/58), [tables](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/45) and [illustrations](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/46).

Structure your content by writing about one idea at a time:

- Start with the most important idea first.
- Group related ideas under [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/51).
- Organise ideas into short [paragraphs](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/53).
- Make sure ideas flow from one paragraph to the next.
- Use a logical order for [sentences](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/120).
rules.violation_condition: Less important ideas precede the most important idea at the start of the content.
context_preconditions: When arranging the ideas in content.

rules.statement: Include the date you are sending the letter so that the recipient knows when you wrote it.
rules.body_excerpt: Include the date you are sending the letter so that the recipient knows when you wrote it. This is especially important if they need to do something or if you are notifying them of a decision.
rules.violation_condition: A letter does not include its sending date.
context_preconditions: The text is a letter.

heading_path: Don’t confuse ordinals with regnal numbers
rules.statement: Even though you might pronounce regnals as ordinal numbers, don't write them like that.
rules.body_excerpt:
Regnal numbers are upper case roman numerals that are used for the titles of monarchs and popes and in family names.

Even though you might pronounce regnals as ordinal numbers, don’t write them like that.
rules.violation_condition: A regnal number is written as an ordinal, including an ordinal suffix attached to a roman numeral.
context_preconditions: Applies to regnal numbers in the titles of monarchs and popes and in family names.
compliant_examples: Elizabeth I
violating_examples: Elizabeth Ist

heading_path: Hyphenate some but not all compound words
rules.statement: Hyphenate compound adjectives consisting of a participle or an adjective.
rules.body_excerpt:
- a government-owned facility
- a heart-rending image
- airborne
- everlasting
- widespread

Hyphenate compound adjectives consisting of a participle or an adjective.
rules.violation_condition: An attributive compound adjective containing a present or past participle lacks a linking hyphen, despite not being an established single word or another explicit exception.
context_preconditions: The expression functions as a compound adjective before a noun.
Established single-word compounds such as airborne, everlasting and widespread are exceptions.
The -ly-adverb rule and degree-modifier rule take precedence.
Ordinary phrases after the noun follow the positional rule.
compliant_examples: a government-owned facility
widespread
airborne
a well-known book
a fast-flowing river
everlasting
a heart-rending image

heading_path: Scan-read table data and text for alignment
rules.statement: Include the unit in the heading if it is not in the title or caption.
rules.body_excerpt:
The text and data in a table are as important as the structure. Align data and text so the table is easy to scan.

In general:

- Align text to the left.
- Align numbers to the right.

In addition, decimal points in the column should line up.

Text should be set horizontally so it is easy to read. Don’t rotate text to display vertically.

If you can, use a fixed-width font for numbers in columns to help users scan the column and compare the values.

For column and row headings:

- Align column headings with the content in the column.
- Include the unit in the heading if it is not in the title or caption.
- Left-align row headings.
rules.violation_condition: A table presents measurements without identifying their unit in the applicable heading or in the title or caption.
context_preconditions: The data has a unit of measurement.
A unit already supplied in the title or caption need not be repeated in the heading.

heading_path: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals
rules.statement: Write 'century' and 'centuries' in lower case.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use numerals, not words, for centuries. This is an exception to the rule for [ordinal numbers](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/ordinal-numbers#use_words_for_ordinals_up_to_ninth_and_numerals_for_10th_and_above).

Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.

Don’t use shortened forms, such as 18C or C18, unless you have limited space.

Don’t use superscript for the ordinal suffix.
rules.violation_condition: The generic word ‘century’ or ‘centuries’ is capitalised within a sentence.
context_preconditions: Normal sentence-initial capitalisation and proprietary names are not generic mid-sentence uses.

heading_path: Show that formulas and some text have special meaning
rules.statement: The name is in italics excluding any definite article.
rules.body_excerpt: Ships, trains, aircraft and other vehicles sometimes have a proper name. The name is in italics excluding any definite article. The brand or type of vehicle is in roman type.
rules.violation_condition: A vehicle’s proper name lacks italics, or its definite article, brand or type is italicised as vehicle-name formatting.
context_preconditions: The text gives the proper name of a ship, train, aircraft or other vehicle.
Any definite article is excluded from the italics.
A vehicle brand or type uses roman type.
compliant_examples: Qantas uses Australian names like Great Southern Land for the Dreamliner fleet.
Until 1997, Queen Elizabeth II would use the Britannia to sail to official visits overseas.

heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
rules.statement: In most cases, it's best to use the division symbol (÷).
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the division symbol (÷) or the division slash ( ∕ ). People sometimes use the forward slash (/) to show division as well.

Use [non-breaking spaces](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/mathematical-relationships#use_a_nonbreaking_space_to_keep_characters_and_symbols_together) around the division symbol.

Programming languages and Excel use the forward slash (/) for division.

In most cases, it's best to use the division symbol (÷). The division slash is easily confused with the forward slash which is also used to show alternatives.

In Unicode, the symbol for division is U+00F7 and the division slash is U+2215.

However, division slashes might appear in expressions you have to reproduce in your content – for example, in algebraic fractions.

The division slash is unspaced. This is a style convention in mathematics. But consider adding a narrow no-break space around the division slash to make the expression clearer. You can also use a thin space, but it will break across lines.

The Unicode characters are:

- division symbol – U+00F7
- division slash – U+2215
- narrow no-break space – U+202F
- thin space – U+2009.
rules.violation_condition: Ordinary division is written with a less-preferred slash notation where there is no reason to preserve an existing slash expression.
context_preconditions: The division symbol and division slash are both permitted mathematical notation.
Division slashes may need to be reproduced from existing expressions, for example algebraic fractions.
The descriptions of forward slashes in programming languages and Excel are not instructions to rewrite software syntax.

heading_path: Write metadata that explains the page
rules.statement: be different on each page
rules.body_excerpt:
The title tells users and search engines what a page is about.

The title should:

- include keywords
- be different on each page
- be 70 characters or fewer.

Titles that are too long will get cut off by search engines.

In a search result, the title is usually the first line. It works as a headline in the search results.
rules.violation_condition: The same page title is reused on different pages of a website.
context_preconditions: Requires comparison with titles of other pages on the website.

rules.statement: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters.
rules.body_excerpt:
News media, industry and government use X (formerly Twitter) for networking, news and public commentary.

X is a platform for current content. Use X to tap into current events, news and positive stories.

The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol. Hashtags help people find and follow topics of interest. If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.

You need no more than 2 hashtags. Too many hashtags makes your content difficult to read and less accessible.

Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags. The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

Address other users with the @ sign before their username. Remember, these tweets are public and visible.
rules.violation_condition: A tweet exceeds the stated maximum of 280 characters.
context_preconditions: Applies to tweets on X (formerly Twitter), as described on this page.

heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms
rules.statement: Don't use commas with Latin shortened forms
rules.body_excerpt: If you use [Latin shortened forms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/91), such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is followed by a comma.
compliant_examples: Exports of rare earths (e.g. lithium, europium) have soared.
violating_examples: Exports of rare earths (e.g., lithium and europium) have soared.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals
rules.body_excerpt:
The academic and professional titles held by individuals usually have initial capitals. This includes honorary titles.

Use lower case if you use a title generically.
rules.violation_condition: A non-generic academic or professional title is written with a lower-case initial where it identifies an individual before their name, replaces their name as an official title, addresses them directly, or forms part of a full title.
context_preconditions: Includes honorary titles and shortened forms of titles.
Applies to non-generic titles immediately before a name.
Applies to official titles replacing a name, direct address and correspondence salutations.
Applies to titles after a name only when they form part of a full title.
Generic titles are checked under the lower-case rule instead.
compliant_examples: ‘We note your concerns Doctor. Thank you for bringing this evidence before the committee’.
All general surgeons at the hospital attended Wednesday’s forum.
Adjunct Professor Monty Chiratte
We welcome Dr Jamilah Mulyadi to our clinic. Dr Mulyadi is now available for skin examinations.
Our new vice-chancellor and president is Professor Rufus Black.
Dear Chancellor
The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Tasmania visited last week.

heading_path: Shortened state and territory names for addresses
rules.statement: write the last line in capitals
rules.body_excerpt: When addressing a letter, write the last line in capitals without punctuation or underlining, with the postcode last. The last line should contain the place name or post office of delivery, state or territory abbreviation and postcode.
rules.violation_condition: The final delivery line of an Australian letter address contains lower-case letters.
context_preconditions: Applies to the letter-address line containing the delivery place or post office, state or territory and postcode.

rules.statement: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding 's' or 'es'.
rules.body_excerpt: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
rules.violation_condition: A plural topographic name is formed by something other than adding the appropriate ‘s’ or ‘es’ ending to the name.
context_preconditions: Applies when referring to multiple places bearing the same topographic name.
compliant_examples: There are 4 Mount Wellingtons in Australia but only one Mount Coot-tha.
There are 3 Mount Jameses in Australia. There is one in Queensland, one in South Australia and one in Western Australia.

heading_path: Use numerals with the percentage sign
rules.statement: Use numerals with the percentage sign
rules.body_excerpt: Use the percentage sign next to a numeral in text. Don’t use a space between the number and the percentage sign.
rules.violation_condition: A numerical percentage is written without numerals and the percentage sign, outside the exceptions for sentence beginnings and imprecise everyday expressions.
context_preconditions: Applies to numerical percentages in text.
At the start of a sentence, the percentage can be written out in words instead.
Everyday words can replace a percentage when a precise amount is not needed.

heading_path: Speak to the person, not their difference
rules.statement: Avoid using words such as 'ethnic Australians' or 'ethnic groups'.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person, not their difference. In Australia, it’s the law.

Commonwealth laws include:

- [*Racial Discrimination Act 1975*](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A00274)
- [*Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986*](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A03366)
- [*Public Service Act 1999*](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A00538).

Mention people’s cultural affinity or identity only when you need to.

Australians speak many different languages and have different cultural and religious beliefs. Each culture has its own values and beliefs. You can be sensitive to these differences when you write, through doing [user research](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/76).

Avoid using words such as ‘ethnic Australians’ or ‘ethnic groups’. This can imply that migrant heritage or migrant status is unusual.
rules.violation_condition: People are labelled ‘ethnic Australians’ or ‘ethnic groups’, or comparable wording presents migrant heritage or migrant status as unusual.
context_preconditions: Apply when labelling people or groups in the Australian cultural-diversity context.

heading_path: Write all numbers as numerals in these specific situations
rules.statement: the correct operator characters
rules.body_excerpt:
Use well-understood conventions to write [mathematical relationships](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/145). Keep relationships together so they are easily understood. To do this use:

- numerals only
- the correct operator characters
- spacing between numerals and operators
- non-breaking spaces.
rules.violation_condition: A mathematical relationship uses a character that is not the conventional operator character for the intended operation.
context_preconditions: Applies to operators in mathematical relationships.

rules.statement: Use Geoscience Australia's authorised abbreviations.
rules.body_excerpt:
Mt Tennent is part of Namadgi National Park.

Spell out the names of other topographic features if you can. Use the abbreviated form only where there’s limited space or a lot of repetition, such as in tables and maps.

Use Geoscience Australia’s [authorised abbreviations](http://www.ga.gov.au/mapspecs/topographic/v6/section2.html#AuthorisedAbbreviations).
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviated topographic feature term uses a form that is not authorised by Geoscience Australia.
context_preconditions: Applies when a topographic feature term is abbreviated.
compliant_examples: Keppel Bay Is
C Tribulation
Green Is
Murray R
L Burley Griffin

rules.statement: Use a single space before and after each ellipsis.
rules.body_excerpt: Use a single space before and after each ellipsis.
rules.violation_condition: An ellipsis lacks the required single-space separation from surrounding text, has multiple separating spaces, or is separated by a space from a following final question mark or exclamation mark.
context_preconditions: Normally require one space before and after the ellipsis.
Do not insert a space between the ellipsis and a following final question mark or exclamation mark.
A terminal ellipsis may directly precede a closing quotation mark, as shown in the Correct example.
An ellipsis representing an omitted paragraph or more may stand alone on a line.
compliant_examples: The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but …’
He asked, ‘What does the Army do during exercises …?’
The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but it needs … more work.’
violating_examples: The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but…’
The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but it needs…more work.’

heading_path: Use the correct term when referring to diplomats
Address high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios with ‘His Excellency’ or ‘Her Excellency’
rules.statement: Address high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios with 'His Excellency' or 'Her Excellency'
rules.body_excerpt: Use ‘His Excellency’ or ‘Her Excellency’ to address high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios.
rules.violation_condition: A high commissioner’s, ambassador’s or nuncio’s style of address accompanying their name omits ‘His Excellency’ or ‘Her Excellency’.
context_preconditions: Applies to styles of address accompanying the names of high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios.
Email and letter salutations follow the separate formal and informal opening requirements.
compliant_examples: His Excellency Mr Tim Kane, Ambassador to Brazil
Her Excellency Ms Francesca Tardioli, Ambassador of Italy
His Excellency Archbishop (Most Rev) Adolfo Tito Yllana, Apostolic Nuncio for Holy See
Her Excellency the Hon Dame Annette Faye King, High Commissioner for New Zealand

heading_path: People who are deaf or hard of hearing
rules.statement: The World Federation of the Deaf disapproves of the term 'hearing impaired' as it describes people as if they have a deficiency.
rules.body_excerpt:
The terms ‘deaf’ and ‘hard of hearing’ include people with no hearing or limited hearing. They might have difficulty using audio content. If you are providing audio content, make the information available in other ways – such as captions and a transcript.

The World Federation of the Deaf disapproves of the term ‘hearing impaired’ as it describes people as if they have a deficiency.

Refer to someone with hearing loss as a ‘person who is deaf or hard of hearing’.

Some people who are deaf or hard of hearing use the Australian sign language, Auslan. Some people who are deaf or hard of hearing view themselves as members of a community and language group. This community calls itself the Deaf community, and encourages others to do the same. The Deaf community uses the term with a capital letter ‘D’ as a mark of its identity.

Members of the Deaf community might still use deaf with a lowercase ‘d’ to refer to their hearing.
rules.violation_condition: using the term 'hearing impaired' instead of 'person who is deaf or hard of hearing'

heading_path: Make PDF content accessible to all users
rules.statement: add 'PDF' and file size to meaningful link text.
rules.body_excerpt:
When you publish a PDF:

- provide the content in another format that is accessible
- mark up the PDF with the right tags
- check that assistive technology reads the PDF content in the correct order
- add 'PDF' and file size to [meaningful link text](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/193/#link_to_something_only_if_it_helps_meet_the_users_need).
rules.violation_condition: A link to a PDF has link text that omits 'PDF', the file size, or both.
context_preconditions: The link points to a published PDF.
compliant_examples: A useful resource for law students is Table of abbreviations [PDF 94.35 KB] by Thomson Reuters Australia.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
rules.statement: Always use an initial capital for 'the Cabinet' to show the difference from its generic reference.
rules.body_excerpt: Always use an initial capital for ‘the Cabinet’ to show the difference from its generic reference.
rules.violation_condition: The governmental body referred to as ‘the Cabinet’ is written with a lower-case ‘c’.
context_preconditions: The reference is to the government body, not a generic cabinet.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
compliant_examples: It was a decision by the Cabinet.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
Include captions for all images that are not decorative
rules.statement: Include the HTML <figcaption> element to associate the caption with the image.
rules.body_excerpt:
Add captions for all images, unless they are only decorative.

Use captions to acknowledge the creator or copyright holder of images in captions. Use your organisation’s [referencing style](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/181).

Include the HTML <figcaption> element to associate the caption with the image.
rules.violation_condition: An HTML image caption is not associated with its image using a <figcaption> element.
context_preconditions: Applies to image captions in HTML.

heading_path: Set off most foreign words and phrases
rules.statement: Set off most foreign words and phrases
rules.body_excerpt: Italics contrast words and phrases that are not in English from surrounding text. Foreign words and phrases should generally be avoided in government writing, unless there is no English equivalent.
rules.violation_condition: A foreign word or phrase that has not been absorbed into Standard Australian English is in roman type, or a borrowing that has been absorbed is italicised.
context_preconditions: Foreign words and phrases in surrounding English text generally use italics.
Borrowings absorbed into Standard Australian English use roman type (accent marks are the borrowed-words rule's, c17746b9a4abe3ab).
Latin shortened forms are the Latin-forms rule's (76404fb918b0d1fe) and First Nations words the First Nations italics rule's (64ee03b12320747d); neither is flagged here as well.
compliant_examples: The more things change, plus c’est la même.
John was the head barista at the department’s coffee shop.

heading_path: Confirm privacy rules before you write to someone
rules.statement: With emails, explain in the covering text that the email has a letter attached.
rules.body_excerpt:
For letters you send electronically:

- Consider using secure messaging services like myGov rather than email.
- With emails, explain in the covering text that the email has a letter attached.

Electronic letters are more accessible for some people than paper letters. For example, a person who is blind or has low vision can access electronic documents by using screen-reading software.
rules.violation_condition: An email carrying an attached letter does not mention the attached letter in its covering text.
context_preconditions: A letter is attached to the email.

heading_path: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to form a possessive shortened form
Don’t use a possessive when defining a shortened form
rules.statement: Don't use a possessive when defining a shortened form
rules.body_excerpt:
Define a shortened form the first time you use it (unless you’re certain users will understand it without a definition). Follow the spelt-out term with its shortened form in parentheses.

Avoid using a possessive apostrophe when you do this. It can be difficult to decide where to put the apostrophe and the sentence is often harder to read.

Use the shortened form rather than the full term if you mention the term again.
rules.violation_condition: A term and its parenthesised shortened form are introduced in a possessive construction.
context_preconditions: The sentence defines a shortened form by giving the spelt-out term followed by the shortened form in parentheses.
This does not prohibit possessive shortened forms after they have been defined.
compliant_examples: The Department of Veterans’ Affairs (DVA) has information about veteran support officers on its website. DVA supports …
violating_examples: Find information about veteran support officers on the Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ (DVA’s) website. DVA supports …

heading_path: Link to something only if it helps meet the user’s need
Include document title, file type and size when linking to files
rules.statement: Include document title, file type and size when linking to files
rules.body_excerpt:
Provide content in [HTML format by default](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/content-formats/reports#consider_publishing_format). This has benefits for both accessibility and maintenance. If a full HTML version of the file is not available, link to a summary page if it exists.

There will be some situations in which you need to link to non-HTML documents and files. Give users the information they need to decide whether to download the file by providing the:

- document title (not the file name)
- the file type
- the file size in kilobytes (kB) or megabytes (MB).

Include all this information in the link text, but remember that this adds extra information for all users. Minimise the number of links where you can.
rules.violation_condition: A non-HTML file link lacks the document title, file type, or file size in kB or MB within its link text, or substitutes the file name for the document title.
context_preconditions: Applies to links to non-HTML documents and files.
All the required information belongs in the link text.
compliant_examples:
You can read more about our financial position in the
Digital Transformation Agency Annual Report 2019–20
[PDF 1.98 MB]
.

heading_path: Choose the right word and spell it correctly
rules.statement: Write 'judgement' rather than 'judgment'.
rules.body_excerpt:
Write ‘judgement’ rather than ‘judgment’.

The exception is a court decision; write this as ‘judgment’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Judgment’ is used for a non-court sense, or ‘judgement’ is used for a court decision.
context_preconditions: Use ‘judgement’ for senses other than a court decision.
Use ‘judgment’ for a court decision.
compliant_examples: Please cite the High Court’s most recent judgment in the issues paper.
You can speak to one of our counsellors without fearing judgement.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.
rules.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.
rules.violation_condition: A personal name has incorrect initial capitalisation, taking account of the person's own usage and the established capitalisation of any particles.
context_preconditions: Applies to real and fictitious people's names.
Preserve deliberately non-capitalised personal forms, such as bell hooks and kd lang.
For names containing particles, use the capitalisation the person uses rather than assuming that every particle needs an initial capital.
Sentence-initial particles are covered by the separate sentence-position rule.
Initials and nicknames have their own more specific capitalisation rules.
compliant_examples: Minjee Lee
Thomas de la Condamine
Clive James
Miles Franklin
Fiona Katauskas
King O’Malley
Dame Constance D’Arcy
Kim van Netten
Freda Du Faur
Oodgeroo Noonuccal
Julian Van Aalst
Beatie Bow

heading_path: Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited
rules.statement: Use a non-breaking space between each time value instead.
rules.body_excerpt:
- 35s
- 6hs
- 15mins
- 5d
- 3wks
- 8mo
- 2y or 2yr
- [There are no non-breaking spaces between numbers and units. There is an ‘s’ after ‘min’, ‘hr’ and ‘wk’.]

But don’t space a number and its unit when your expression contains more than one time measure. Use a non-breaking space between each time value instead.

Never add an ‘s’ to show a plural.
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent time-value components in a compound shortened-unit expression are not separated by a non-breaking space.
context_preconditions: Applies to expressions containing more than one shortened time measure.
System-specific data formats may have their own requirements.

heading_path: Organise heading levels in a logical order
rules.statement: Space out headings
rules.body_excerpt: Separate each heading from the next one by some text, even if it’s only a sentence. This helps create a clear distinction between ideas.
rules.violation_condition: Two successive headings have no explanatory text between them.
context_preconditions: Even a single sentence between headings is sufficient.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
Write alt text and captions to support the image’s purpose
rules.statement: For logos that are functional links to home pages, use the name of the site in the link instead of the alt text.
rules.body_excerpt:
Write the full name of the organisation in the logo alt text.

For logos that are functional links to home pages, use the name of the site in the link instead of the alt text. You don’t need to add the name to the link if it is already in the text on the page.
rules.violation_condition: A logo linking to a home page supplies the site name only in alt text instead of in the link, or omits the required site name from the link when it is not already on the page.
context_preconditions: Applies only to logos that link to home pages.
The site name need not be added to the link if it is already in the text on the page.

heading_path: Scan-read table data and text for alignment
rules.statement: In addition, decimal points in the column should line up.
rules.body_excerpt:
The text and data in a table are as important as the structure. Align data and text so the table is easy to scan.

In general:

- Align text to the left.
- Align numbers to the right.

In addition, decimal points in the column should line up.

Text should be set horizontally so it is easy to read. Don’t rotate text to display vertically.

If you can, use a fixed-width font for numbers in columns to help users scan the column and compare the values.

For column and row headings:

- Align column headings with the content in the column.
- Include the unit in the heading if it is not in the title or caption.
- Left-align row headings.
rules.violation_condition: Decimal points in a numeric table column are not vertically aligned.
context_preconditions: The column contains numbers with decimal points.

rules.statement: Put the publication details for each issue on the cover page.
rules.body_excerpt:
Put the publication details for each issue on the cover page. Include:

- the title
- the publishing date
- the sponsoring body
- the volume and part number (if any).

Put this extra information on page 2 (with the contents list) or the back page:

- the name of the printer, publisher, distributor or agent
- the editorial address
- subscription rates.

Start each issue of a periodical without a separate cover from page 1. Include the title, date and page number at the top or bottom of the page.
rules.violation_condition: The cover page of an issue without a separate cover is missing the title, publishing date, sponsoring body or applicable volume and part number.
context_preconditions: Applies to print periodicals without separate covers.
Volume and part numbers are required only if the publication has them.

heading_path: Use graphs, charts and maps if they explain complex information
Refer to informational images in the text
rules.statement: Ensure your text comments on or interprets the image, rather than repeating the text or data in it.
rules.body_excerpt:
The photograph of an ideal workstation set-up (see left) shows an example of good ergonomic posture.

Ensure your text comments on or interprets the image, rather than repeating the text or data in it.
rules.violation_condition: Text accompanying an image merely repeats its text or data without commenting on or interpreting it.
context_preconditions: When discussing information displayed in an image.
compliant_examples: European Union expenditure more than quadrupled from 2016 to 2018 (Figure 7).
violating_examples: Figure 7 shows European Union expenditure increased from US$9 million in 2016 to about US$40 million in 2018.

heading_path: Capitalise the same way as the spelt-out version
rules.statement: Capitalise the same way as the spelt-out version
rules.body_excerpt: Use the same capitalisation as for the unabbreviated word.
rules.violation_condition: An abbreviated word has different capitalisation from the corresponding unabbreviated word.
compliant_examples: misc for ‘miscellaneous’
Dec for ‘December’

heading_path: Create a list rather than use ordinals
Ordinals in journals and other publications
rules.statement: 'Firstly' and 'secondly' work as a pair. Don't use one without the other.
rules.body_excerpt:
Ordinals, such as ‘firstly’ and ‘secondly’, are sometimes used in content written for government publications such as journals and reports. In this type of content, they order thoughts without interrupting the flow of the text.

‘Firstly’ and ‘secondly’ work as a pair. Don’t use one without the other.
rules.violation_condition: A thought sequence uses ‘firstly’ without ‘secondly’, or ‘secondly’ without ‘firstly’.
context_preconditions: Applies where ordinal thought sequencing is used in journals, reports or other government publications.
The two markers must belong to the same thought sequence; unrelated occurrences elsewhere do not form a pair.
compliant_examples: The committee responded in 2 ways. Firstly, they asked for an immediate adjournment of proceedings. Secondly, they sought clarification about their powers to subpoena witnesses.
violating_examples: The committee responded in 2 ways. They asked for an immediate adjournment of proceedings. Secondly, they sought clarification about their powers to subpoena witnesses.

rules.statement: Choose words that respect all people, including their rights and their heritage.
rules.body_excerpt: People can relate to content when it uses [inclusive language](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/178). Choose words that respect all people, including their rights and their heritage.
rules.violation_condition: Wording refers to people in a way that disrespects them, their rights or their heritage.

heading_path: Shortened forms for titles immediately before a name
rules.statement: Only use shortened forms of titles in limited circumstances.
rules.body_excerpt:
Only use shortened forms of titles in limited circumstances. People might understand common contractions like ‘Prof’ for ‘Professor’, but some shortened forms are confusing. For example, the initialism for ‘Pro Vice-Chancellor’ is ‘PVC’. To ensure your content is readable, write the title in full.

Shortened forms are sometimes necessary because of limited space. For example, shortened forms often appear in tables. List the full form of any title that people might find confusing in a [note](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/structuring-content/tables#add_notes_to_provide_sources_or_help_interpret_the_data).

The space available for image captions can be limited, but write the full names and titles as a default. If you have to use initials and the shortened forms of titles in a caption, always include the full forms in body text to provide context.

‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances. Like ‘Ms’ and ‘Mr’, ‘Dr’ is easy to understand when it appears before a name.
rules.violation_condition: An academic or professional title other than ‘Dr’ is shortened in body text, or is shortened elsewhere without a limited-circumstances justification.
context_preconditions: Applies to shortened titles immediately before a name.
Limited space can justify shortened forms outside body text, including in tables and image captions.
Body text must use the full form except for ‘Dr’.
‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances.
compliant_examples: This year’s graduate cohort asked Deputy Vice-Chancellor Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.
Left to right: Assoc Prof S Baird, VC T Dhillon, Dean F Ealing, Adj Prof O Iraklidis, Dr C Nieminen

Departmental officers recently attended Upsilon University’s annual Copyright Symposium. The academic panel (pictured below), chaired by Vice-Chancellor Tom Dhillon, discussed recent cases with implications for fair dealing provisions of the Copyright Act 1968.
Left to right: Associate Professor Sara Baird, Vice-Chancellor Tom Dhillon, Dean Frank Ealing, Adjunct Professor Olena Iraklidis, Dr Celia Nieminen
violating_examples: DVC Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
Use consistent formatting and punctuation for captions and titles
rules.statement: Capitalise the first word and proper nouns only.
rules.body_excerpt:
Align captions and titles to the left. Place captions for decorative images, such as photographs, below the image.

Titles and captions don’t need to be a complete sentence. Other grammar and punctuation rules for titles and captions are:

- Capitalise the first word and proper nouns only.
- Don’t use a full stop to end the title or caption, even if it is a complete sentence.

All titles and captions should have the same:

- structure (parallel structure)
- terms and shortened forms as those used in the rest of the content (such as [acronyms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/190))
- font and typeface.
rules.violation_condition: A title or caption has an uncapitalised first word or proper noun, or capitalises other words as title case.
context_preconditions: Applies to image titles and captions.
In numbered titles, the title text after the label and colon begins with a capital.

heading_path: Write common names in lower case and roman type
rules.statement: Use roman type for the names of proteins (enzymes).
rules.body_excerpt:
When using genetic terms for plants and animals:

- Use italics for the names of genes.
- Use roman type for the names of proteins (enzymes).

Capitalisation varies for the names of genes, but proteins usually take an initial capital only.
rules.violation_condition: A plant or animal protein or enzyme name is italicised.
context_preconditions: Applies to genetic terms for plants and animals.
The occurrence must name the protein or enzyme, not its gene.

heading_path: Address members of the ADF by rank, name and post-nominals
rules.statement: If you mention the name again in body text, use rank and family name.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Rear Admiral Robert W Plath AM RAN
- Lieutenant General Susan Coyle AM CSC DSM
- Air Marshal Mel Hupfeld AO DSC
- [Don’t use commas]

If you mention the name again in body text, use rank and family name.
rules.violation_condition: A subsequent body-text reference to an ADF member is not in rank-and-family-name form.
context_preconditions: The member has already been named in the body text.
This concerns a repeated name, not a pronoun referring to the member.
compliant_examples: Chief Petty Officer Ray Rosendale CSM is a Kuku Yalanji man of the Western Sunset Clan. He was born in Nambour and joined the Navy in 1991. Chief Petty Officer Rosendale now has a role advising the Navy on First Nations cultural affairs.
Chief Petty Officer Rosendale now has a role advising the Navy on First Nations cultural affairs.

heading_path: Follow the guidance on capitals for titles and government terms
rules.statement: Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder.
rules.body_excerpt:
Follow conventions for using capitals for [titles, honours and forms of address](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/149). Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder. This includes titles for executives specified in legislation.

Unless advised in this manual, avoid using capitals in body text for a particular position or role within an organisation. This practice goes against readability and does not support clarity.

You do not need to use capitals when the title is an organisational name given to an office holder. Deference for positions within an organisation might follow house style. Do not use house style outside of the organisational context. Detail any special use of capitals in a [style sheet](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/169#a_style_sheet_is_a_useful_tool).

Preferences for capitals when the terms ‘traditional owner’, ‘elder’ and ‘custodian’ are used as titles should come directly from the relevant [First Nations community](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/179#style_for_first_australian_languages_needs_to_recognise_continuing_cultures).
rules.violation_condition: An official title preceding its office holder's name lacks the capitals required for that title.
context_preconditions: An official title precedes the office holder's name.
Includes titles for executives specified in legislation.
Capitalisation is not required merely because a title is an organisational name given to an office holder.

Titles of ministers, departmental secretaries and parliamentary office holders and members are government-terms.md's rules (e2495e194ebd6a93, 0aad7c36d7cdb33a, 61ac4d74adfcc3f6, ff27ed43128e97bf), so they are not flagged here as well.
compliant_examples: Chief Defence Scientist Tanya Monro presented the award ...

heading_path: Write one exclamation mark: don’t overuse them
rules.statement: At the end of each sentence you want to emphasise, use only one exclamation mark.
rules.body_excerpt:
Don’t use exclamation marks too often. Exclamation marks can lose their emphasis if you use too many.

At the end of each sentence you want to emphasise, use only one exclamation mark.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence ends with more than one exclamation mark used for emphasis.
context_preconditions: Applies when exclamation marks are used to emphasise a sentence.
Applies to government social media content as well as other government content.
Does not apply to exclamation marks displayed as literal characters rather than sentence punctuation.
compliant_examples: Were you born overseas or have a parent who was? Nearly half of Australians do!
violating_examples: Were you born overseas or have a parent who was? Nearly half of Australians do!!!

heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
rules.statement: Separate the numbers and the initialism with a non-breaking space.
rules.body_excerpt:
The initialisms ‘am’ and ‘pm’ come from the Latin phrases *ante meridiem* (before noon) and *post meridiem* (after noon).

Write ‘am’ and ‘pm’ in lower case. Separate the numbers and the initialism with a non-breaking space.

Don’t use ‘am’ and ‘pm’ with words that duplicate their meaning, for example ‘morning’ and ‘afternoon’.
rules.violation_condition: A time number and its am or pm designation are not separated by a non-breaking space.
context_preconditions: Applies to 12-hour times with am or pm.

heading_path: Use <label> or <legend> for digital form headings
rules.statement: If you have one question per page, use that question as the heading for the page.
rules.body_excerpt:
If you have one question per page, use that question as the heading for the page.

Put the <label> or <legend> element inside the <h1> element.

This avoids screen readers reading out the same information twice.
rules.violation_condition: A digital form page with one question uses a different page heading instead of the question.
context_preconditions: Applies to digital form pages containing one question.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
rules.statement: Use an initial capital for the word 'federation' only when referring to Australia's Federation in 1901.
rules.body_excerpt: Use an initial capital for the word ‘federation’ only when referring to Australia’s Federation in 1901.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Federation’ is lower case when referring to Australia's Federation in 1901, or has an unnecessary capital when it does not refer to that event.
context_preconditions: References derived from the 1901 event include Federation style architecture.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation is not a violation.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
compliant_examples: The type of architecture popular between 1890 and 1915 is known as Federation style architecture.
The design of Australia’s national flag is the result of a competition announced to coincide with Federation in 1901.

heading_path: Use an en dash for spans in technical content
rules.statement: The en dash is unspaced when it connects only 2 numbers.
rules.body_excerpt:
In technical content where there are many numbers, you can use en dashes for number, date and page spans. Don’t combine en dashes with ‘from’ or ‘to’ in the spans.

The en dash is unspaced when it connects only 2 numbers.
rules.violation_condition: A technical-content span consisting of 2 numbers has spaces around its connecting en dash.
context_preconditions: Applies to numerical, date and page spans in technical content.
The dash connects only 2 numbers.
compliant_examples: There were 25–30 head of cattle in quarantine in June and 50–60 in July.
Air quality declined during the 2003–2006 reporting period.
This same result was reported in Smith and Jones (2020:5–15).

heading_path: Set column and row headings that are clear and accurate
rules.statement: If you use a complex table, you must define the column and row groups and mark up the table accordingly.
rules.body_excerpt:
Complex tables have header cells that span more than one column or row. If you use a complex table, you must define the column and row groups and mark up the table accordingly. This is so screen reader users can access the information in the table.

For detailed instructions and tutorials, visit:

- W3C’s web accessibility tutorial ‘[Tables with irregular headers](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/irregular/)’
- Adobe’s [*PDF accessibility repair: examine and repair tables*](https://www.adobe.com/accessibility/products/acrobat/pdf-repair-repair-tables.html).
rules.violation_condition: A complex table lacks definitions and corresponding markup for its column or row groups.
context_preconditions: A complex table has header cells spanning more than one column or row.

heading_path: Don’t write dates as numerals unless space is limited
rules.statement: Use 2 digits for the day and month and 4 digits for the year: 'dd.mm.yyyy'.
rules.body_excerpt: Many computer systems and applications use a full stop in numeric dates. Use 2 digits for the day and month and 4 digits for the year: ‘dd.mm.yyyy’.
rules.violation_condition: A full-stop numeric date in a computer-system or application context is not written as dd.mm.yyyy.
context_preconditions: Applies where a computer system or application uses full stops in numeric dates.

heading_path: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
rules.statement: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
rules.body_excerpt:
Post-nominals are letters after a name that stand for academic, civil and military [awards and honours](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/titles-honours-forms-address/awards-and-honours).

Make sure you write post-nominals [in the right order](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/titles-honours-forms-address/awards-and-honours#use_postnominals_in_the_correct_order).

Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.
rules.violation_condition: Post-nominal letters are placed before the person’s name rather than after it.
context_preconditions: Post-nominals are included in an academic or professional title.

rules.statement: If it's not clear and you can't ask them, choose gender-neutral pronouns.
rules.body_excerpt:
Learn the user’s [pronoun](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/131). If it’s not clear and you can’t ask them, choose gender-neutral pronouns.

The singular ‘they’ is gender-neutral. It avoids specifying a person’s gender.

You can use ‘they’ or ‘them’ when you would otherwise use a singular personal pronoun such as:

- ‘he’
- ‘she’
- ‘him’
- ‘her’.

You can also use ‘themselves’ or ‘themself’ instead of ‘himself’ or ‘herself’. ‘Themself’ is an extension of using ‘they’ for a single person.

The use of gender-neutral pronouns to refer to a person of unknown gender has a long history. Usage now covers people who either:

- don’t wish to identify as a particular gender
- identify as non-binary or gender-fluid.

There are many ways to avoid using gender-specific pronouns.
rules.violation_condition: A gender-specific pronoun refers to a person whose pronoun is unclear and who cannot be asked.
context_preconditions: Applies when the person’s pronoun is unclear and it is not possible to ask them.
Singular ‘they’ and ‘them’ are permitted.
Both ‘themselves’ and ‘themself’ are permitted for a single person.
Rewriting with second-person pronouns, a plural subject or no pronoun is also acceptable.
compliant_examples: Candidates must provide copies of the application to their referees.
You must provide copies of the application to your referees.
Every candidate must provide copies of the application to referees.

heading_path: Use shortened forms for dates when space is limited
rules.statement: Don't use a full stop after shortened days and months.
rules.body_excerpt:
Only use abbreviations if space is limited – for example, in tables, illustrations, charts and notes. Ensure that it is obvious to users which days of the week or months you are referring to.

The standard abbreviations for the days of the week are:

- Monday – ‘Mon’ or ‘M’
- Tuesday – ‘Tues’ (‘Tue’) or ‘Tu’
- Wednesday – ‘Wed’ or ‘W’
- Thursday – 'Thurs’ (‘Thur’,‘Thu’) or ‘Th’
- Friday – ‘Fri’ or ‘F’
- Saturday – ‘Sat’ or ‘Sa’
- Sunday – ‘Sun’ or ‘Su’.

The abbreviations in parentheses are alternatives for the standard abbreviation they follow. Only use the alternatives when the context ensures their meaning is clear.

Note: Style Manual lists Monday as the first day of the week. This is consistent with the order of calendar days in a calendar week as defined in the international standard adopted by Australia.

The standard abbreviations for the months are:

- January – ‘Jan’
- February – ‘Feb’
- March – ‘Mar’
- April – ‘Apr’
- May – retain as ‘May’
- June – retain as ‘June’ or shorten to ‘Jun’
- July – retain as ‘July’ or shorten to ‘Jul’
- August – ‘Aug’
- September – ‘Sept’ or shorten to ‘Sep’
- October – ‘Oct’
- November – ‘Nov’
- December – ‘Dec’.

Only use the shortest form
rules.violation_condition: A shortened day or month name has a full stop marking the abbreviation.
context_preconditions: A sentence-ending full stop is not an abbreviation full stop.

heading_path: Explain acronyms and initialisms to all users
Spell out most acronyms on first use
rules.statement: Spell out most acronyms on first use
rules.body_excerpt: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention. Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form needing explanation lacks a definition at first mention, or its introduction lacks the required full-term/shortened-form pairing and parentheses in the appropriate order.
context_preconditions: Applies to acronyms and initialisms at their first mention.
Define the shortened form if there is a chance users will not know its meaning.
A definition is unnecessary if all users will understand the shortened form without one.
For well-known forms that are explained, put the shortened form first and the full term in parentheses.
Examples not needing a first-use definition include NT, ACT, am, pm, BHP and Qantas.
Words in their own right, such as radar, scuba and sonar, do not need first-use definitions.

An organisation's name at first mention is organisation-names.md's rule (39fdaf50ef1682c9), and explanatory material bills-and-explanatory-material.md's (5a9855fcff9fcf66), so they are not flagged here as well.
compliant_examples: The Department of Social Services (DSS) manages a range of benefits and payments for eligible Australians. DSS helps support communities through a number of programs and services.
All living organisms have DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) within their cells. DNA tells cells what proteins to make.

heading_path: Use the correct style for equations
rules.statement: There is no space between a character and its superscript or subscript.
rules.body_excerpt:
An equation is a statement or question consisting of 2 mathematical expressions linked by an equals symbol (=).

Use equations if user research supports their inclusion.

The Unicode character for the equals symbol is U+003D.

Put a [non-breaking space](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/mathematical-relationships#use_a_nonbreaking_space_to_keep_characters_and_symbols_together) around the equals symbol and around all operators except for the division slash – it is unspaced. If you think the equation is clearer with a space around the division slash, use a narrow no-break space (U+202F) or thin space (U+2009).

There is no space between a character and its superscript or subscript.
rules.violation_condition: Whitespace separates a character from its superscript or subscript.
context_preconditions: The adjacent material is a superscript or subscript belonging to the character.
compliant_examples: xa × xb = xa+b
xn = xn-1 + xn-2
violating_examples: x a × x b = x a+b
x n = x n-1 + x n-2

heading_path: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
rules.statement: it's better to say 'register a trade mark'.
rules.body_excerpt:
The trade mark Vegemite was first registered in 1923.

You should also spell ‘trade mark’ as 2 words when you use it as a verb, although it’s better to say ‘register a trade mark’.
rules.violation_condition: The verb ‘trade mark’ is used to describe registration rather than wording with ‘register’, such as ‘register a trade mark’ or ‘register your brand as a trade mark’.
context_preconditions: When describing registration using ‘trade mark’ as a verb.

rules.statement: Always use the first entry in the list.
rules.body_excerpt:
Government organisations should choose one dictionary of Australian English.

This manual recommends either:

- the *Australian concise Oxford dictionary*(ACOD)
- the *Macquarie dictionary*.

Use your organisation’s preferred dictionary as a spelling reference when you write. Spelling and word usage can change over time. Make sure you use an up-to-date edition that reflects current language usages.

Dictionaries include any variable spellings for words. Always use the first entry in the list. This helps to ensure words are spelt consistently in government content.

Only use an alternative spelling listed for a word if you have evidence it will meet a [user need](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/user-needs/understanding-needs/user-research-and-content). Record decisions you make about alternative spellings in a [style sheet](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/general-conventions-editing-and-proofreading/editing-and-proofreading#a_style_sheet_is_a_useful_tool).

The entry for a spelling can expand on changes to the basic form of a word. These changes show things like the plural, past tense, or the root from which a word is formed. These changes are called ‘infle
rules.violation_condition: A later-listed spelling variant is used instead of the selected dictionary’s first-listed spelling, without evidence that the alternative meets a user need.
context_preconditions: Applies where the selected dictionary lists alternative spellings of the same word.
An alternative listed spelling is permitted where there is evidence that it meets a user need.
Consistent use of an accepted dictionary may produce spellings different from those used in the Style Manual.
Specific Style Manual guidance for a term or phrase takes precedence over the dictionary default.
Quoted material keeps its original spelling, US spellings included (quotation-marks.md, 7ce25fb67fe032ad).

heading_path: Nationalities, peoples and places outside Australia
Check the official status for area and region names
rules.statement: Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.
rules.body_excerpt: Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.
rules.violation_condition: The name of a recognised political or geographic region lacks its required initial capitals.
context_preconditions: For names of groups of nations or areas recognised as political or geographic regions.
Recognition can include well-known names that have gained semi-official status.
An initial capital is not required when a name is used generically.
compliant_examples: Central America
North Africa
Kurdistan
the Balkans

rules.statement: Don't use more than 2 levels.
rules.body_excerpt:
Multilevel lists group information into a hierarchy. The levels explain how each item relates to other list items.

Some types of content need multilevel lists, but they can be hard for people to follow.

If you have to use multilevel lists:

- Don’t use more than 2 levels.
- Use lowercase letters for the second level in a numbered list.
- Use a dash for the second level in a bullet list, not hollow (open) bullets.
- Use the same symbol, number or letter for the same level in each list.
rules.violation_condition: A multilevel list has three or more levels.
context_preconditions: Applies when a multilevel list is used.

heading_path: Follow the possession rules for different types of nouns
rules.statement: Follow the possession rules for different types of nouns
rules.body_excerpt:
To correctly show possession by using an apostrophe, first ask, ‘Who or what is doing the possessing?’

The apostrophe goes straight after the noun that is the answer.

There are possession rules for using an apostrophe, according to the [type of noun](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/122).

| Noun type | Rule | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Singular noun | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ | the committee’s report
our department’s plan
the bus’s passengers
the kibbutz’s energy needs |
| Singular noun of 2 or more words, the last word being a plural ending in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe only | the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ office
a Department of Social Services’ project
the United States’ representatives |
| Plural nouns that end in letter ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe only | both committees’ reports
the Joneses’ submission
the Sanchezes’ security passes |
| Plural nouns that don’t end in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ | our children’s education
the sheep’s wool
the gateaux’s boxes |
| Proper names ending in letter ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe and another ‘s’, even if you don’t pronounce that final ‘s’ | Burns’s report
James’s profession
Laos’s population
Louis’s supervisor
Jesus’s disciple
rules.violation_condition: A possessive noun has a missing or incorrectly formed possessive ending, or the ending is attached inside rather than after the complete noun or compound.
context_preconditions: Singular nouns take an apostrophe and s.
A singular noun of 2 or more words whose last word is a plural ending in s takes an apostrophe only.
Plural nouns ending in s take an apostrophe only; other plural nouns take an apostrophe and s.
Proper names ending in s take an apostrophe and another s, regardless of pronunciation.
For compounds, put the ending after the complete compound and choose the ending according to whether the compound ends in plural s.
Possessive shortened forms take an apostrophe and s; plural shortened forms ending in s take an apostrophe only.
Singular time references take a possessive apostrophe.
Descriptive phrases, possessive pronouns, plural time phrases and possessive Australian place names are governed by their separate rules.
Preserve an organisation’s official apostrophe usage.
For coordinated possessors, this rule checks the form of endings that are present; the joint and individual possession rule checks which owners require an ending.
compliant_examples: our children’s education
Smith and Miller’s report
the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ office
Smith’s and Miller’s offices
the committee’s report
both committees’ reports
Burns’s report

rules.statement: Avoid imperial units
rules.body_excerpt:
Don’t use imperial units of measurement in Australia unless you have a specific reason, such as:

- in quotations from historical documents
- when writing for readers in countries (particularly the United States) where imperial measures, or elements of them, still apply.
rules.violation_condition: Imperial measurements are used in Australian content without a specific contextual reason.
context_preconditions: Applies to content for use in Australia.
Historical quotations can retain imperial units.
Imperial units can be appropriate for readers in countries where those measures remain in use.
The page also presents fuel gallons, oil barrels, screen inches and aircraft-altitude feet as examples in this exception discussion.
compliant_examples: gallons for volume of fuel
inches for the size of a screen
barrels for volume of oil
In the 1970s, the speed limit for highways in many states of Australia was set at 60 miles per hour (97 km/h).
feet for the altitude of a plane

heading_path: Use tables if they make content easier to read
rules.statement: If it is numeric data, use the numeric zero (0).
rules.body_excerpt:
User needs:

- I can change the content without losing information or structure.
- I can find and navigate the content and determine where I am on the webpage.

Fundamentals:

- Tables can be made accessible for all users. The World Wide Web Consortium has [tips for setting up tables](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/tips/).
- You must give a table:
- a title (also called a [caption](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49))
- row and column headings
- information (entries)
- a cross-reference in the text.
- You may also need to add notes below the table to help users understand the information and where it comes from.
- Don’t rely on colour as the only visual means of conveying information in tables.
- Don’t leave cells empty. Use ‘zero’ or ‘nil’ or 'n/a' where there is no data. If it is numeric data, use the numeric zero (0). Only use zero if that is the true value.

WCAG quick reference:

- [1.3.1 Info and relationships – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#info-and-relationships)
- [1.4.1 Use of color – level A](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/#use-of-color)
rules.violation_condition: A true zero in numeric table data is written as a word rather than as 0.
context_preconditions: The entry is numeric data with a true value of zero.

heading_path: Subordinate clauses depend on the main clause
rules.statement: When you're writing, choose the right one:
rules.body_excerpt:
‘If’ and ‘whether’ are both subordinating conjunctions. They can often be interchangeable, particularly in spoken English. Yet they have different meanings. When you’re writing, choose the right one:

- ‘If’ is conditional. It defines a condition that needs to exist for the main clause to be true.
- ‘Whether’ shows 2 possibilities. Sometimes one of the possibilities can be understood rather than explicitly mentioned.
rules.violation_condition: ‘If’ or ‘whether’ expresses a relationship inconsistent with the intended meaning established by context: a condition governing the main clause versus a choice between possibilities.
context_preconditions: The words are used as subordinating conjunctions.
‘If’ introduces a condition needed for the main clause to be true.
‘Whether’ introduces possibilities; one possibility may be implied.
The words can often be interchangeable, particularly in spoken English; interchangeability alone is not a violation.
compliant_examples: We can choose whether to eat lunch outside or inside.
We asked whether the office was open [or not].
We asked whether he was working from home or from the office.
We asked if he was working from home or from the office.
We can eat lunch outside if the rain stops.

heading_path: Hyphenate some but not all compound words
rules.statement: Use a hyphen in compound nouns made up of a verb plus an adverb.
rules.body_excerpt: Use a hyphen in compound nouns made up of a verb plus an adverb. This shows that the adverb is part of the compound rather than modifying other elements of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A compound noun made from a verb followed by an adverb lacks the linking hyphen.
context_preconditions: The combination functions as a noun, rather than as a verb phrase.
The verb precedes the adverb.
The reverse order, adverb then verb, does not require a hyphen.
compliant_examples: the go-ahead for the project
bypass
downpour
a shake-out
input
some make-up
uproar

heading_path: Use the correct form to refer to judges and magistrates
rules.statement: Refer to judges of the following courts as 'Justice'
rules.body_excerpt:
Refer to judges of the following courts as ‘Justice’ and use the title ‘The Honourable’:

- High Court
- Federal Court
- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1)
- supreme courts in the states and territories.

Use the titles ‘Your Honour’, ‘His Honour’ or ‘Her Honour’ for judges of:

- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)
- district courts
- county courts.
rules.violation_condition: A formal reference to a serving judge of a listed court lacks the judicial designation ‘Justice’, including as part of ‘Chief Justice’.
context_preconditions: Applies to judges of the High Court, Federal Court, Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1), and state and territory supreme courts.
The lifetime retention provisions concern ‘The Honourable’; they do not require retired judges to retain ‘Justice’.
Email and letter salutations are covered by the separate salutation rule.
compliant_examples: The Honourable Susan Kiefel AC
The Honourable Justice Christine Mead
The Hon Justice Penelope Neskovcin
The Honourable Justice Joshua Wilson
The Hon Justice Dowling
The Honourable Chief Justice Stephen Gageler AC

heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
rules.statement: Use numerals for times of day
rules.body_excerpt:
In most documents, numerals give a clearer expression of time. Write times of day using numerals, especially when you need to convey precise times.

Use a colon between the hours and minutes. The use of a colon as the separator, rather than a full stop, reflects a shift in contemporary Australian usage.

A colon ensures that the time isn’t confused with a decimal number.

For example, ‘10.50’ can be read as ‘10 and a half’ as well as ‘50 minutes past 10’. Screen reader users will probably hear ‘10.50’ as ‘10 point 5’.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinary time-of-day expression spells out its numerical time components in words.
context_preconditions: Particularly applies when precise times must be conveyed.
Noon, midday and midnight are the prescribed word forms for those times.
When ‘o’clock’ is allowed in a quotation or transcription, its hour is still written as a numeral.

heading_path: Choose the right word and spell it correctly
for all intents and purposes/for all intensive purposes
rules.statement: The correct expression is 'for all intents and purposes', meaning 'in every practical sense'.
rules.body_excerpt: The correct expression is ‘for all intents and purposes’, meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.violation_condition: The expression is written as ‘for all intensive purposes’.
context_preconditions: When using the expression meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
compliant_examples: The paperwork may take a few weeks to come through but, for all intents and purposes, you are hired.

heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
rules.statement: Write the initialism 'UTC', followed by '+' or '−', followed by the time offset to UTC in 24-hour system format.
rules.body_excerpt:
Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is a time standard used as the basis for regulating world timekeeping.

UTC expresses the unadjusted local time at 0° longitude. It is not adjusted for daylight saving. Local standard time at longitudes around the world is represented by an offset to UTC.

UTC is based on International Atomic Time (TAI), which is a weighted average of atomic clocks located around the world, including in Australia. TAI does not take into account changes in the earth’s rotation, so leap seconds are occasionally added to UTC.

UTC is the standard and legal reference for times of day in Australia. The UTC(AUS) standard is maintained by the Australian Government’s [National Measurement Institute](https://www.industry.gov.au/national-measurement-institute).

Time zones are written as positive or negative offsets to UTC.

Write the initialism ‘UTC’, followed by ‘+’ or ‘−’, followed by the time offset to UTC in 24-hour system format.
rules.violation_condition: A written UTC offset does not have UTC followed by a plus or minus sign and the offset in 24-hour system format.
context_preconditions: Applies when expressing a time zone as an offset to UTC.
The examples use UTC+HH:MM and UTC−HH:MM.

rules.statement: Use gender-specific adjectives only when gender is relevant.
rules.body_excerpt:
- actress
- hostess
- waitress
- stewardess

Gender is not relevant to a person’s profession or title in general. Use gender-specific adjectives only when gender is relevant. For example, an economic analysis might discuss ‘female-dominated’ or ‘male-dominated’ industries.
rules.violation_condition: A gender-specific adjective is used even though gender is irrelevant to the subject being discussed.
context_preconditions: Gender-specific adjectives are allowed when gender is relevant.
An economic analysis discussing female-dominated or male-dominated industries is an expressly permitted context.

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: Use the heading 'Contents', not 'Table of contents' or 'List of contents'.
rules.body_excerpt:
A list of contents helps the user to get an overview of the report. In HTML, this can often inform the menu navigation.

Use the heading ‘Contents’, not ‘Table of contents’ or ‘List of contents’.

There is rarely a need to use more than 3 levels of headings. Use design elements such as colour or typeface size for complex contents. This can separate the levels of heading and show the structure of the report. Make sure design elements are accessible.
rules.violation_condition: The contents list is headed ‘Table of contents’ or ‘List of contents’, rather than ‘Contents’.
context_preconditions: The report has a list of contents.

heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for a period of time
rules.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for a period of time
rules.body_excerpt:
Noun phrases about plural time periods don’t need apostrophes because they’re usually descriptive, not possessive.

In phrases such as ‘6 months retired’ or ‘5 months pregnant’, the time periods are clearly adjectival. They don’t show possession.

Other noun phrases aren’t possessive because they are conversational shorthand for an ‘of’ phrase. For example, ‘in 4 days time’ is shorthand for ‘in 4 days of time’.

Some styles use an apostrophe to stand for the word ‘of’ and don't use it for descriptive phrases. For many years, the Style Manual has recommended the simple rule of no apostrophe for either use.
rules.violation_condition: A phrase about a plural time period contains a possessive apostrophe, whether the phrase is descriptive or shorthand for an of phrase.
context_preconditions: Applies to plural time periods.
Covers descriptive uses and conversational shorthand for an of phrase.
Singular time references instead take an apostrophe under the possessive-ending rule.
compliant_examples: a day’s work
the year’s cycle

heading_path: Write compass points in lower case
rules.statement: no full stops or hyphens.
rules.body_excerpt:
- south
- north-east
- west-north-west
- A north-westerly wind was blowing the fire towards the town.
- The car was 30 degrees east of where it should have been.
- A cool change was coming from the south.

You can use initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works. Always use capital letters with no full stops or hyphens.
rules.violation_condition: A compass-point initialism contains a full stop or hyphen.
context_preconditions: Applies to compass-point initialisms.
The page permits these initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works.
A sentence-ending full stop after an initialism is not punctuation within the initialism.

heading_path: Use brackets for text users can skip over
rules.statement: These are specialist uses, so don't use them in most content.
rules.body_excerpt:
Brackets can help you break up information. They enclose parts of the sentence that aren’t essential to the meaning. Sentences must be grammatically correct if you remove the text in brackets.

The most commonly used brackets are:

- parentheses
- square brackets.

Use brackets sparingly for:

- non-essential information
- [shortened forms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/92)
- references
- insertions.

Use brackets only where they make content clearer to people. For example, always use brackets in [author–date citations](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/165#examples_of_authordate_citations).

Too many brackets, or badly used brackets, can make a sentence more complex and difficult to understand. You can usually rewrite a sentence so the content in brackets can be its own sentence or can even be removed.

Other types of brackets, such as curly brackets and slant brackets, are used in fields such as mathematics and linguistics. These are specialist uses, so don’t use them in most content.
rules.violation_condition: Ordinary, non-specialist content uses specialist bracket types such as curly brackets or slant brackets.
context_preconditions: Specialist uses, such as those in mathematics and linguistics, are exceptions.

heading_path: Italicise specific names and use capitals
rules.statement: Italicise specific names and use capitals
rules.body_excerpt:
Write the names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles:

- in italics
- with initial capitals.

This makes the name of the ship, aircraft or other vehicle clear. The name contrasts with the rest of the sentence.

Don't use the definite article for navy ships.
rules.violation_condition: An individual ship, aircraft or other vehicle name is written with a lowercase initial where its name requires an initial capital.
context_preconditions: Applies to the proper names of individual vehicles.

The heading also requires italics; that half is the italics page's vehicle-name rule (52758d37d95259ec), which this page's own detailed guidance backs, so an unitalicised name is flagged there and not here as well.
compliant_examples: HMAS Canberra is the Royal Australian Navy’s flagship.
Australian–American astronaut Andy Thomas flew his first flight in space aboard the Endeavour.
The Indian Pacific travels 4,532 kilometres from Perth to Sydney.

rules.statement: 'sighted person' for someone who is not blind
rules.body_excerpt:
- person with a disability
- handicapped person
- handicapped parking
- crippled
- invalid
- incapacitated
- mad
- mute
- deaf and dumb
- deaf person
- blind person
- person without sight

You can cause offence when you do not use respectful language, even if it is well intentioned.

- Don’t say a person is inspirational only because of their disability.
- Don’t write about people as if they are heroes or victims.
- Avoid euphemisms and made-up terms, such as ‘differently abled’ and ‘handicapable’.

People with disability could consider these types of terms condescending.

When you are making comparisons, write:

- ‘person without disability’ – rather than ‘able-bodied’
- ‘sighted person’ for someone who is not blind
- ‘hearing person’ for someone who is not deaf.
rules.violation_condition: A comparison uses a label other than ‘sighted person’ for someone who is not blind.
context_preconditions: Applies when labelling someone who is not blind in a comparison involving blindness.
Ordinary grammatical variants, such as ‘sighted people’, retain the prescribed terminology.

rules.statement: You need no more than 2 hashtags.
rules.body_excerpt:
News media, industry and government use X (formerly Twitter) for networking, news and public commentary.

X is a platform for current content. Use X to tap into current events, news and positive stories.

The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol. Hashtags help people find and follow topics of interest. If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.
