You need no more than 2 hashtags. Too many hashtags makes your content difficult to read and less accessible.

Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags. The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

Address other users with the @ sign before their username. Remember, these tweets are public and visible.
rules.violation_condition: A post contains more than 2 hashtags.
context_preconditions: Applies to posts on X (formerly Twitter).
This is an upper limit, not a requirement to include hashtags.

heading_path: A descriptive phrase doesn’t need an apostrophe
rules.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for these nouns.
rules.body_excerpt:
Some nouns are descriptive rather than possessive. In a descriptive noun phrase, the first noun modifies the second noun by operating as a [definitive adjective](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/types-words/adjectives#there_is_a_common_order_for_strings_of_adjectives).

Don’t use an apostrophe for these nouns.

The first noun is essential to the meaning of the second noun. For this reason, never separate the nouns in a descriptive phrase.
rules.violation_condition: The modifying noun in a descriptive noun phrase carries a possessive apostrophe even though it identifies a type rather than a possessor.
context_preconditions: The first noun describes or classifies the second noun rather than expressing possession.
The manual explicitly treats workers compensation, meaning the insurance, as descriptive.
Some agencies require an apostrophe in workers compensation under their house styles; the page acknowledges but does not recommend that style.
Plural time phrases have a separate, more specific rule.
Official organisation names retain their official apostrophe usage.
compliant_examples: workers compensation
visitors book
drivers licence

heading_path: Quantify an amount of money with a symbol and numeral
rules.statement: Don't use a full stop after the 'c' unless it's at the end of a sentence.
rules.body_excerpt:
- $27.99

For an amount less than $1, you can write it either as a whole number of cents or as a [decimal value](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/146#use_0_before_a_decimal_point_for_values_less_than_one).

For the cents form:

- Use the letter ‘c’ for cents after the numerals.
- Don’t add a space between the numerals and the ‘c’*.*
- Don’t use a full stop after the ‘c’ unless it’s at the end of a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The cents suffix ‘c’ is followed by a full stop that is not sentence-ending punctuation.
context_preconditions: Applies to ‘c’ used as the cents suffix.
A full stop is allowed when it ends the sentence.

rules.statement: A hyphen precedes '-fold' when that suffix is used with a numeral, but not a spelled out number.
rules.body_excerpt:
readable

colourful

costly

A hyphen precedes ‘-fold’ when that suffix is used with a numeral, but not a spelled out number.
rules.violation_condition: The suffix fold lacks a hyphen after a numeral or has a hyphen after a spelled-out number.
context_preconditions: Fold is a numerical suffix.
Numeral bases take a hyphen.
Spelled-out number bases do not take a hyphen.
compliant_examples: threefold
300-fold

heading_path: Use sentence lists for a series of complete sentences
rules.statement: Start each list item with a capital letter
rules.body_excerpt:
If you have a paragraph with a series of related sentences, you can consider breaking it into a sentence list.

Sentence lists have a list of sentences, each marked by bullets or numbers.

The list can have a:

- heading (without a colon or full stop)
- sentence lead-in (ending in a colon or full stop)
- phrase lead-in (ending in a colon).

Rules for sentence lists:

- Follow normal sentence structure in each list item.
- Start each list item with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
- Align run-over lines with the text, not the bullet or number.

Avoid using multiple sentences in each bullet or numbered item. If you include more than one sentence per list item, consider whether:

- all list items conform to a similar pattern
- the list builds [rhythm for readability](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/60#rhythm_changes_can_help_or_hinder_reading).
rules.violation_condition: A sentence-list or stand-alone-list item starts in lower case, or a fragment-list item starts with a capital despite not beginning with a proper noun.
context_preconditions: Sentence-list and stand-alone-list items start with a capital letter.
Fragment-list items start in lower case unless the first word is a proper noun.

heading_path: Use en dashes for particular types of year spans
rules.statement: Always include the phrases 'financial year', 'financial years', 'calendar year' or 'calendar years' unless the context makes the meaning clear.
rules.body_excerpt:
Government content often includes spans of years. Some year spans are easier to read and understand if they contain an unspaced en dash rather than words.

This is particularly true in content that contains multiple spans of years. In this case, using en dashes makes the content easier to scan.

Use an unspaced en dash for a:

- financial year
- calendar year
- span of years in the titles of publications and programs
- span of years written in parentheses, such as for a term of office and the years of birth and death.

Always include the phrases ‘financial year’, ‘financial years’, ‘calendar year’ or ‘calendar years’ unless the context makes the meaning clear. You can also introduce the relevant phrase at first mention and just write the year span, without the phrase, in later mentions.

Finally, exercise your judgement. Consider using en dashes for year spans when using words makes the content harder to read.
rules.violation_condition: A financial-year or calendar-year span is presented without identifying which kind of year it denotes, and the context does not make that meaning clear.
context_preconditions: The identifying phrase may be introduced at first mention and omitted from later mentions.
The phrase is unnecessary if the meaning is already clear from context.

heading_path: Alt text, captions and titles for images
Use consistent formatting and punctuation for captions and titles
rules.statement: terms and shortened forms as those used in the rest of the content (such as acronyms)
rules.body_excerpt:
Align captions and titles to the left. Place captions for decorative images, such as photographs, below the image.

Titles and captions don’t need to be a complete sentence. Other grammar and punctuation rules for titles and captions are:

- Capitalise the first word and proper nouns only.
- Don’t use a full stop to end the title or caption, even if it is a complete sentence.

All titles and captions should have the same:

- structure (parallel structure)
- terms and shortened forms as those used in the rest of the content (such as [acronyms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/190))
- font and typeface.
rules.violation_condition: An image title or caption uses terms or shortened forms inconsistent with the rest of the content.
context_preconditions: Read the quoted item under ‘All titles and captions should have the same:’.

heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Don’t use a symbol or a space for ratios
rules.statement: Ratios don't have a space around the colon.
rules.body_excerpt:
Ratios don’t use a symbol, unlike mathematical operators. Ratios use a punctuation mark instead: the [colon](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/104).

Ratios don’t have a space around the colon.
rules.violation_condition: Whitespace appears immediately before or after the separator in a ratio.
context_preconditions: Applies to ratio notation, not to other uses of a colon.

heading_path: Use capitals for proper nouns and genus names
rules.statement: Always refer to organisations in the same way as they refer to themselves.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Lou Gehrig’s disease [Named after Lou Gehrig, a high-profile person who had the disease]
- Legionnaires’ disease [Named after members of the American Legion – known as Legionnaires – who were the first documented people to have the disease]
- Alzheimer disease [Named after Dr Alois Alzheimer, who first described the disease]
- Down syndrome [Named after Dr John L H Down, who first described the syndrome]
- Henle loop [Anatomical part named after anatomist Gustav Jakob Henle]

This rule doesn’t apply to names of organisations dedicated to studying certain diseases or supporting people who are affected by them. Always refer to organisations in the same way as they refer to themselves.
rules.violation_condition: The name of a disease-related organisation is written differently from the organisation’s own form, including changing its possessive form to match the medical-eponym convention.
context_preconditions: In this context, applies to names of organisations dedicated to studying diseases or supporting people affected by them.
compliant_examples: Crohn’s & Colitis Australia
Alzheimer’s Association

heading_path: Meet standards for data systems and information interchange
rules.statement: If you use dates in electronic data transfer, use basic format and don't separate the numbers.
rules.body_excerpt:
Ordinal dates are often used when transferring data between data systems. This is because they are easy for simple systems to read.

Ordinal dates are not the same as [ordinal numbers](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/ordinal-numbers).

Ordinal dates have 7 digits:

- The first 4 digits represent the year.
- The next 3 digits represent the day.

This is the ISO standard. Some older systems might use 2 digits for the year, not 4.

Days are numbered from 1 to 365 (366 for a leap year). For example, 20 September is the 263rd day of the year (264th in a leap year) and its 3 digits are 263.

The ordinal date can be unspaced (basic format) or separated by a hyphen (extended format).

If you use dates in electronic data transfer, use basic format and don’t separate the numbers.

If people, rather than a computer, will read the information, use extended format and insert a hyphen between the year and day.
rules.violation_condition: An ordinal date uses a separator in electronic data transfer, or omits the year–day hyphen when presented for people to read.
context_preconditions: This instruction is in the ordinal-date subsection.
Use unseparated basic format for electronic data transfer.
Use extended format with a hyphen between year and day for human readers.

heading_path: Finalise the script before you start recording
Language and tone in audio-only content
rules.statement: Use simple language and a conversational tone, and avoid jargon.
rules.body_excerpt:
Because audio-only content isn’t supported by images, language and tone of voice are important:

- Use simple language and a conversational tone, and avoid jargon.
- Don’t over-simplify to the point where you lose meaning and people feel patronised.

A conversational tone also helps the speakers inject their personalities into the script. Follow Australian Public Service values, regardless of the topic.
rules.violation_condition: Audio-only wording uses a non-conversational tone.
context_preconditions: Applies to the verbal wording of audio-only content, not the acoustic qualities of a recording.

heading_path: If age is relevant, follow style conventions
rules.statement: When the reference to age comes before a noun, punctuate it with hyphens.
rules.body_excerpt:
Question whether age is relevant. Avoid referring to a person’s age or an age group if it’s not relevant.

If you need to mention age, follow style conventions:

- When the reference to age comes before a noun, punctuate it with [hyphens](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/105).
- Unless the age reference begins a sentence, use [numerals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/198).
rules.violation_condition: An age expression modifying a following noun is missing a required hyphen.
context_preconditions: The age expression comes before and modifies a noun.
The instruction also applies when the age is written in words at the beginning of a sentence.
compliant_examples: A 39-year-old man faces court today on several charges.
Fourteen-year-old Jasmine Greenwood is the youngest Australian on the Paralympic Games squad.

heading_path: Requirements and standards for video and audio
Include subtitles or captions for video
Centre subtitles and captions at the bottom of the screen
rules.statement: start each line with a dash
rules.body_excerpt:
If there are 2 speakers:

- give each speaker a separate line and start each line with a dash
- align each line to the left of the subtitle block so that their left edges stack above each other
- centre the whole subtitle or caption block.

Don’t use a full stop at the end of subtitles. Use an ellipsis to indicate the end of a sentence where speech trails off or where a sentence remains unfinished.

Use italics for:

- foreign words and phrases
- dialogue that is not on the screen, such as a public announcement or dialogue from a television program.

A hash symbol (#) or a quaver symbol (♪) show song lyrics.
rules.violation_condition: A speaker’s line in a caption or subtitle with 2 speakers does not start with a dash.
context_preconditions: A caption or subtitle block contains 2 speakers.

heading_path: Be concise when writing about percentages
rules.statement: When you use many percentages in body text, put the figures in brackets (parentheses) or use a list to simplify the text.
rules.body_excerpt: When you use many percentages in body text, put the figures in brackets (parentheses) or use a list to simplify the text.
rules.violation_condition: Body text contains many percentages in running prose without putting the figures in parentheses or presenting them in a list.
context_preconditions: Applies to body text containing many percentages.
Parentheses and a list are alternative acceptable presentations.
compliant_examples: In 2019, population size increased in New South Wales (32%), Queensland (20%) and Victoria (19%).
violating_examples: In 2019, the largest sources of population growth were New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. New South Wales accounted for 32% of the population growth, Queensland 20%, and Victoria 19%.

heading_path: Use graphs, charts and maps if they explain complex information
Refer to informational images in the text
rules.statement: Refer to informational images in the text
rules.body_excerpt:
Refer to complex images in the body of the text. It helps people relate the discussion in the text to the information displayed in the image.

Place the image close to where you mention it in the text. For example, a graph must be on the same page and after the paragraph that refers to it.

Don’t repeat the whole [caption of the image](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49) in the text. Instead, use a locator number to refer to it, for example ‘Figure 1’.

Don’t refer to ‘the photograph on the left’. This sensory language is not accessible for some users.

You don’t need to refer to decorative images and illustrations in the text unless they are part of the discussion.
rules.violation_condition: A complex or informational image (graph, chart, map, diagram) is not referred to anywhere in the body text.
context_preconditions: You don't need to refer to decorative images and illustrations unless they are part of the discussion.

heading_path: Use alt text, captions and titles to explain images
rules.statement: Add alt text to all images.
rules.body_excerpt:
Follow the guidance on adding [alt text, captions and titles](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49).

Add alt text to all images.

Include captions for all images that are not decorative. Add titles to help users scan content.
rules.violation_condition: An image has no alt text at all: no alt attribute (or document alt-text setting), so neither a description nor the deliberate empty value is present.
context_preconditions: A decorative image with the empty value (alt="", or the document's 'Decorative image' setting) is not missing alt text: that empty value is what the decorative-image rule requires (8067ec35218b13f1).
Whether a present description is adequate is the alt-text page's rules, not this one.

heading_path: Write compass points in lower case
rules.statement: Always use capital letters
rules.body_excerpt:
- south
- north-east
- west-north-west
- A north-westerly wind was blowing the fire towards the town.
- The car was 30 degrees east of where it should have been.
- A cool change was coming from the south.

You can use initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works. Always use capital letters with no full stops or hyphens.
rules.violation_condition: A compass-point initialism contains a lowercase letter instead of the required capital letter.
context_preconditions: Applies to compass-point initialisms.
The page permits these initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works.

heading_path: Avoid using a semicolon to link sentences
rules.statement: If you have to use a semicolon, on both sides of the semicolon write full sentences.
rules.body_excerpt:
Find out if it’s optional or compulsory before you start; ask someone to help you if you don’t know the difference.

Too much punctuation makes text crowded and difficult to read. If a sentence has a lot of punctuation marks, it might be a sign that the sentence is too long or complex. Try to rewrite into [shorter, clearer sentences](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/204).

If you have to use a semicolon, on both sides of the semicolon write [full sentences](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/120). Other than in some sentence lists, it’s incorrect to have a sentence fragment on one side of the semicolon.
rules.violation_condition: A semicolon used to link sentences has a sentence fragment on either side.
context_preconditions: Applies to semicolons linking sentences.
Does not apply to semicolons separating items in the sentence lists described later on the page.
compliant_examples: Staff can leave at any time; they don’t need a work schedule.
violating_examples: Staff can leave at any time; no work schedule.

heading_path: Be consistent: use a parallel structure
rules.statement: Be consistent: use a parallel structure
rules.body_excerpt:
All headings in a level should be consistent.

They should have the same:

- overall message (for example, they are all steps in a process)
- grammatical form (called ‘parallel structure’).

Two common forms are:

- noun phrases (for example, ‘effective headings’ and ‘punctuation and capitalisation’)
- instructions (for example, ‘keep headings short’ and ‘be consistent’).
rules.violation_condition: Headings at the same level use inconsistent grammatical forms, such as mixing noun phrases and instructions.
context_preconditions: Compare headings at the same level.

heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
rules.statement: It always uses at least 4 digits.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the 24-hour clock if it helps people understand your content. This is important when referring to times in these contexts:

- travel
- certain scientific fields
- the armed services
- content written for countries using the 24-hour clock.

The 24-hour clock is also useful in content where space is limited. This is because it uses fewer characters than times with ‘am’ and ‘pm’. For this reason, it is often used in timetables and schedules.

This system numbers the hours from 00:00 hours (midnight) to 23:59. It always uses at least 4 digits. It can have 6 digits if seconds are included:

- The first 2 digits are the hours.
- The next 2 digits are the minutes.
- The last 2 digits are the seconds, if you include them.

Always use a ‘leading zero’ for hours under 10 – for example, write ‘05:30’ not ‘5:30’.

Use a colon to separate the hours, minutes and seconds in the 24-hour clock.
rules.violation_condition: A 24-hour time does not contain two-digit hour and minute components, or has a seconds component that is not two digits.
context_preconditions: A 24-hour time has HHMM components, with optional SS.
Hours below 10 require a leading zero.
Separators are governed by the separate time-separator rule.
Also applies to the numeric components of ISO local-time representations.

heading_path: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives
Separate adjectives of the same type
rules.statement: Don't use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.
rules.body_excerpt:
- This is an ethical, profitable, efficient organisation. [Descriptive adjectives]
- They were a happy, caring, devoted workforce. [Evaluative adjectives]

Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.
rules.violation_condition: Commas separate adjectives of different types (evaluative, descriptive, definitive) in a string before a noun (‘my new, black, felt-tip pen’).
compliant_examples: We found some used French tennis balls left over from a training day.
My new black felt-tip pen splattered ink everywhere.

heading_path: Address certain office holders of the Australian Parliament as ‘Honourable’
rules.statement: Use the title 'Senator' before 'the Honourable' if the minister or parliamentary secretary is a member of the Senate.
rules.body_excerpt:
- The Hon Chris Bowen MP, Minister for Climate Change and Energy [Serving minister]
- The Hon Darren Chester MP [Serving MP and former minister]
- The Hon Michelle Landry MP [Serving MP and former assistant minister]

Use the title ‘Senator’ before ‘the Honourable’ if the minister or parliamentary secretary is a member of the Senate.
rules.violation_condition: A federal senator entitled to Honourable has the title sequence reversed or otherwise lacks ‘Senator’ before ‘the Honourable’ or ‘the Hon’.
context_preconditions: Applies to federal ministers and parliamentary secretaries who are senators.
The examples include senators retaining Honourable after ministerial or assistant ministerial service.
Hon is a permitted abbreviation of Honourable.
compliant_examples: Senator the Hon Jonathon Duniam
Senator the Hon Bridget McKenzie

rules.statement: Introduce block quotations with colons
rules.body_excerpt: Use a colon to introduce a block quotation. Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.
rules.violation_condition: A block quotation's lead-in does not end with a colon.
context_preconditions: A lead-in introduces a block quotation.
compliant_examples:
For example, Manthorpe (2019) stated:
Short sentences are easier to read because they limit the scope of an idea. But most readers like the variety and rhythm of a mixture of sentence lengths. For most readers, aim for an average sentence length of 15 words per sentence.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for words in the formal name.
rules.body_excerpt:
To refer to an Australian state or territory:

- Use initial capitals for words in the formal name.
- Use lower case for generic or plural references.
rules.violation_condition: An Australian state or territory's formal name lacks its required capitals, a generic or plural state/territory reference is unnecessarily capitalised, or the semi-official Northern Territory name ‘Territory’ is incorrectly lower case.
context_preconditions: The reference is to an Australian state or territory.
Generic and plural references take lower case.
‘Territory’ takes a capital when used as the semi-official substitute for ‘Northern Territory’, but not when used generically.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
compliant_examples: The South Australian Government started the project. The government will meet regularly to review progress.
The Territory is a common destination for overseas tourists.
The Australian Capital Territory has a land border length of 306 kilometres. The territory’s total area is more than 2,000 square kilometres.
The states and territories are responsible for health care and education.
The Northern Territory road toll is a concern to the territory.

rules.statement: Don't ask for a title or gender identity unless the form is designed to collect this information.
rules.body_excerpt:
‘Ms’ is now widely used instead of ‘Mrs’ or ‘Miss’. It does not disclose marital status.

‘Mx’ refers to non-binary people and those who do not wish to be referred to by their gender. Use ‘Mx’ when a person indicates this is what they prefer, but not otherwise.

Forms and surveys can ask for people to specify gender. Don’t ask for a title or gender identity [unless the form is designed to collect this information](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/177). For example, a form can ask for [a person’s given and family name](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/59). It does not need to ask for their preferred title.
rules.violation_condition: A form requests a title or gender identity even though collecting that information is outside the form’s purpose.
context_preconditions: Forms specifically designed to collect the requested title or gender-identity information are excepted.
The guidance also discusses surveys.

heading_path: Don’t end contractions with full stops
rules.statement: Grammatical contractions use only one apostrophe, even if the contraction leaves out letters from more than one place.
rules.body_excerpt:
- Tempo Australia Ltd hired him last year. [No full stop after the contraction]
- He is currently working for Tempo Australia Ltd. [A full stop after the contraction ends the sentence.]
- They said they can’t! [No full stop after the contraction because another punctuation mark ends the sentence]

Australian practice differs from US English, which adds a full stop after a contraction (for example, ‘Mr.’, ‘Ltd.’).

Don’t use an apostrophe to show missing letters in a contraction of a single word (‘Dr’, ‘Ltd’). Grammatical contractions use only one apostrophe, even if the contraction leaves out letters from more than one place.
rules.violation_condition: A grammatical contraction contains more than one apostrophe to mark omitted letters.
context_preconditions: Applies to grammatical contractions joining two words.
Omission of letters from multiple places does not justify additional apostrophes.
compliant_examples: shan’t
violating_examples: sha’n’t

heading_path: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Respectful language use starts with the basics
rules.statement: possessive terms such as 'our', as in 'our Aboriginal peoples'
rules.body_excerpt:
Basic respectful language means using:

- specific terms, like the name of a community, before using broader terms
- plurals when speaking about collectives (peoples, nations, cultures, languages)
- present tense, unless speaking about a past event
- empowering, strengths-based language.

Language that can be discriminatory or offensive includes:

- shorthand terms like ‘Aborigines', ‘Islanders’ or acronyms like ‘ATSI’
- using terms like ‘myth’, ‘legend’ or ‘folklore’ when referring to the beliefs of First Nations people
- blood quantums (for example, ‘half-caste’ or percentage measures)
- ‘us versus them’ or deficit language
- possessive terms such as ‘our’, as in ‘our Aboriginal peoples’
- ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’, as it also implies ownership, much like ‘our’.

Many texts have referred to First Nations people in the past tense, for example:

- ‘The Aboriginal language existed for hundreds of years.’
- ‘Torres Strait Islanders once congregated at this place.’

This use of past tense continues the historical erasure of First Australians.

The 2 statements also show a lack of understanding about diversity within either group.

Statements to redress the historical erasure and
rules.violation_condition: A reference to First Nations peoples implies ownership of them, including ‘our Aboriginal peoples’ or ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’.
context_preconditions: Assess whether the expression implies ownership of First Nations peoples; do not prohibit every occurrence of a possessive pronoun.

heading_path: Refer to classification systems to help you name plants and animals
Subcategories of species are usually abbreviated
rules.statement: By convention, the abbreviation 'subsp.' is not used.
rules.body_excerpt:
- *Grevillea victoriae* subsp.
- *Grevillea banksii* var.

For animals, there is only one taxonomic level below that of species: subspecies. By convention, the abbreviation ‘subsp.’ is not used.
rules.violation_condition: An animal subspecies name includes the rank abbreviation subsp.
context_preconditions: Applies to animal subspecies names, not botanical names.
compliant_examples: Macropus agilis jardinii is a subspecies of the agile wallaby (M. agilis).

heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Don’t use a symbol or a space for ratios
rules.statement: Ratios use a punctuation mark instead: the colon.
rules.body_excerpt:
Ratios don’t use a symbol, unlike mathematical operators. Ratios use a punctuation mark instead: the [colon](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/104).

Ratios don’t have a space around the colon.
rules.violation_condition: A ratio is written without the colon separator required by the prose, or with a different kind of separator.
context_preconditions: Applies to notation expressing a ratio.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
rules.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
rules.violation_condition: A trade mark, brand or business name written without the capitalisation its owner uses: lower case where the owner uses initial capitals, or 'normalised' capitals where the owner uses an unusual mix (iPhone, nbn, YouTube), including at the start of a sentence.
context_preconditions: If the business writes its name with unusual spacing, capitals or lower case, write it that way.
A name that starts with a lower case letter keeps it at the start of a sentence (eBay).
This is for trade marks, brands and business names as brands. An organisation name written entirely in lower case takes an initial capital in body text (organisation-names.md, 39bda8748c81df79).
compliant_examples: eBay is a popular online auction site.
Harley-Davidson
Collins Class submarine
Instagram
X
YouTube
nbn
iPhone
UNIX

heading_path: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals
rules.statement: Use initial capitals for the actual name of a geological era or period but not for broad historical and cultural times.
rules.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals for the actual name of a geological era or period but not for broad historical and cultural times.
rules.violation_condition: A geological era or period name is lowercased, or a broad historical or cultural descriptor is capitalised as though it were a specific proper name.
context_preconditions: Capitalise the actual geological name, not the generic word ‘era’ or ‘period’.
Use lower case for broad historical and cultural descriptors.

heading_path: Refer to people living in Australia as ‘Australians’
rules.statement: Don't use these words once people have settled and become Australian citizens.
rules.body_excerpt:
Many Japanese take part in the Summer Festival in Melbourne. [Does not convey dual identity of community or individuals]

To refer to people who have recently arrived in Australia, use the words:

- ‘migrants’
- ‘immigrants’
- ‘new arrivals’.

These words don’t say anything about a person’s culture or language: they are neutral. Don’t use these words once people have settled and become Australian citizens. They suggest a temporary or marginal status.
rules.violation_condition: People who have settled in Australia and become Australian citizens are labelled ‘migrants’, ‘immigrants’ or ‘new arrivals’.
context_preconditions: Both settlement and Australian citizenship have occurred.

heading_path: Use keywords in the URL and content
rules.statement: Create URLs that contain words from the title of the page with the main keywords close to the start.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use keywords in the:

- web address (URL, or ‘uniform resource locator’)
- metadata
- [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/51)
- [page content](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/72)
- [internal links](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/193)
- [captions and alt text for images](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/49).

Create URLs that contain words from the title of the page with the main keywords close to the start.

The URL should be below 100 characters and make sense to the user.

To separate words in the URL, use hyphens instead of spaces or underscores. This helps both people and search engines understand each word.
rules.violation_condition: The main keywords occur late in a page URL rather than close to its start.
context_preconditions: Assess the position of the page’s main keywords within its URL.
compliant_examples: https://stylemanual.gov.au/about-style-manual

heading_path: Keep most paragraphs to 2 or 3 sentences
rules.statement: Keep most paragraphs to 2 or 3 sentences
rules.body_excerpt:
Short paragraphs help people understand content. The ideal length depends on what you are writing, for example:

- Media releases and news articles have 1 or 2 sentences in a paragraph.
- Content designed for mobile screens has no more than 2 or 3 sentences in a paragraph.
- Reports (and other long-form content) usually have a limit of 6 sentences in a paragraph.

If your paragraphs or sentences are too long, you might be trying to say too much in one place.

Consider starting a new paragraph or using an [itemised list](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/56). Make sure the items relate to each other and are grammatically parallel.

A paragraph can be one sentence, but be careful. Overusing single-sentence paragraphs reduces their effectiveness and can disrupt the flow of content.
rules.violation_condition: The content does not follow the recommended paragraph-length profile for its type: ordinary prose is not mostly 2 or 3 sentences per paragraph, media or news paragraphs exceed 2 sentences, mobile paragraphs exceed 3, or long-form paragraphs routinely exceed 6.
context_preconditions: Media releases and news articles use 1 or 2 sentences per paragraph.
Content designed for mobile screens has no more than 3 sentences per paragraph.
Reports and other long-form content usually have a limit of 6 sentences per paragraph.
One-sentence paragraphs are permitted, but should not be overused.

heading_path: Use respectful terms when you write about age
rules.statement: Young people
rules.body_excerpt:
The most neutral term is ‘young people’. ‘Youth’ is a gender-neutral term and is also acceptable.

Be careful using the plural ‘youths’. This is often used to refer to male youths only and may carry other connotations.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Junior’ or ‘juniors’ is used as a label for young people.
context_preconditions: ‘Young people’ is the most neutral term; ‘youth’ is also acceptable.
The plural ‘youths’ often refers to male youths only and may carry other connotations: use it with care.
‘Adolescents’, ‘children’, ‘babies’ and, depending on voice and tone, ‘kids’ are acceptable in context.
compliant_examples: The eSafety Commissioner resources for kids and young people are tailored to different reading ages.
youth
young people
violating_examples: junior or juniors

rules.statement: Address other users with the @ sign before their username.
rules.body_excerpt:
News media, industry and government use X (formerly Twitter) for networking, news and public commentary.

X is a platform for current content. Use X to tap into current events, news and positive stories.

The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol. Hashtags help people find and follow topics of interest. If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.

You need no more than 2 hashtags. Too many hashtags makes your content difficult to read and less accessible.

Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags. The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

Address other users with the @ sign before their username. Remember, these tweets are public and visible.
rules.violation_condition: A post addresses another user by username without an immediately preceding @ sign.
context_preconditions: Applies when addressing another user by username on X (formerly Twitter).
Does not require every reference to a person to be a username mention.

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: The letter of transmittal must include the purpose of the report and who it is for.
rules.body_excerpt:
A letter of transmittal is a message or letter to the person requesting the report. It is often included in annual reports and other reports prepared by committees, commissions and consultants. Sometimes it must be part of a report.

The letter of transmittal must include the purpose of the report and who it is for. It must have:

- the signature of the person responsible for the report
- the day, month and year the report was submitted.
rules.violation_condition: A letter of transmittal omits the report's purpose, its intended recipient, the responsible person's signature, or the submission date expressed with day, month and year.
context_preconditions: The report includes a letter of transmittal.
This passage does not identify every report type that must include such a letter.

rules.statement: Don't also use the IBAN currency code.
rules.body_excerpt:
Minimum wages are currently:

- Australia – AUD19.49 per hour
- Thailand – THB313.00 per day
- Vanuatu – VUV220.00 per hour
- Vietnam – VND4.18 million per month (urban Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City).

If using foreign currency symbols:

- Explain them on first use unless they are very widely known (for example, US$).
- Place them before the numerals and don’t insert a space.
- Don’t also use the IBAN currency code.
rules.violation_condition: The same monetary amount is labelled with both a currency symbol and an IBAN currency code.
context_preconditions: Applies to Australian-dollar amounts as well as foreign-currency amounts.
violating_examples:
The minimum wage in the United States is currently
$
7.25
USD
per hour.

heading_path: Use fragment lists for a series of incomplete sentences
rules.statement: Make sure each fragment can complete a phrase lead-in.
rules.body_excerpt:
If you list more than 3 items in a sentence, consider breaking the sentence into a fragment list. This will aid readability.

Fragments are words, phrases or incomplete sentences. Another name for fragment lists is ‘phrase lists’.

Fragment lists have a:

- lead-in phrase or sentence followed by a colon
- list of fragments, each marked by a bullet.

Use fragment list items when the lead-in states the [grammatical subject](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/120#a_full_sentence_is_grammatically_complete).

Rules for fragment lists:

- Use lower case for the first letter of each fragment, unless it’s a proper noun.
- Add a full stop to the last list item only.
- Use a grammatically parallel structure for each list item.
- Make sure each fragment can complete a phrase lead-in.
rules.violation_condition: Combining a fragment-list item with its phrase lead-in fails to produce a complete grammatical sentence.
context_preconditions: Applies to fragment lists with a phrase lead-in.
Each item is tested separately with the lead-in.
compliant_examples:
Queensland is famous for its:
islands and coral reefs
abundant wildlife
tropical rainforest
beautiful beaches.
violating_examples:
Queensland is famous for its:
islands and coral reefs
experience the tropical rainforest
the wildlife. It can kill you.
beautiful beaches.

heading_path: Design headings and other elements to help the user scan the page
rules.statement: Use a logical hierarchy or sequential steps for headings.
rules.body_excerpt:
Once you have decided on the type of structure you need to use, plan the structural elements.

- Use a logical hierarchy or sequential steps for [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/51).
- Write a topic sentence for each [paragraph](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/53).
- Display important information in [lists](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/56), [callout boxes](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/58), [tables](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/45) and [illustrations](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/46).

Structure your content by writing about one idea at a time:

- Start with the most important idea first.
- Group related ideas under [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/51).
- Organise ideas into short [paragraphs](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/53).
- Make sure ideas flow from one paragraph to the next.
- Use a logical order for [sentences](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/120).
rules.violation_condition: The headings express an illogical hierarchy or place sequential steps in an illogical order.
context_preconditions: When organising content with headings.
Either a logical hierarchy or sequential steps can satisfy the instruction.

heading_path: Address mayors and members of local governments with the correct title
rules.statement: Add 'Councillor' before the names of the lord mayors of Brisbane, Hobart, Melbourne and Sydney.
rules.body_excerpt:
Use the title ‘The Right Honourable the Lord Mayor of [the name of the city]’ for lord mayors of:

- Adelaide
- Brisbane
- Hobart
- Melbourne
- Perth
- Sydney.

In emails and letters, you can use either the full form ‘Right Honourable’ or its shortened form ‘Rt Hon’ (without full stops).

Add ‘Councillor’ before the names of the lord mayors of Brisbane, Hobart, Melbourne and Sydney.

Put a comma after the name of the city.
rules.violation_condition: A full address to one of the six specified capital-city lord mayors omits or substitutes the required title before the person’s name.
context_preconditions: For Brisbane, Hobart, Melbourne and Sydney, put Councillor before the lord mayor’s name.
For Adelaide and Perth, use the applicable personal honorific Ms, Mr, Mx, Mrs or Dr with the lord mayor’s name.
compliant_examples: The Rt Hon the Lord Mayor of Adelaide, Dr Jane Lomax-Smith AM
The Right Honourable the Lord Mayor of Melbourne, Councillor Nicholas Reece
The Rt Hon the Lord Mayor of Sydney, Councillor Clover Moore AO

heading_path: Use stand-alone lists for items under a heading
rules.statement: Items cannot be full sentences.
rules.body_excerpt:
If you are not breaking up a paragraph or a sentence, consider a stand-alone list.

Stand-alone lists have a heading without a colon. Brochures and technical documents often contain stand-alone lists.

Items in stand-alone lists can be nouns or noun phrases. They can also be sentence fragments. Items cannot be full sentences.

Rules for stand-alone lists:

- Use a heading, not a lead-in.
- Start each list item with a capital letter.
- Don’t add full stops to the end of any of the list items (even the last item).
- Indent each list item if it helps people scan the content.
rules.violation_condition: A stand-alone list contains full-sentence items rather than nouns, noun phrases or sentence fragments.
context_preconditions: Applies to stand-alone lists.
Nouns, noun phrases and sentence fragments are allowed.
compliant_examples:
My weekly tasks
Answer phone enquiries
Book conference venues
Order stationery
Take meeting minutes

heading_path: Use initial capitals to write about protective markings
rules.statement: Use initial capitals to write about protective markings
rules.body_excerpt: In general content, use an initial capital unless you are reporting how the protective marking actually appears on the page. In that instance, write the marking as it appears and use quotation marks.
rules.violation_condition: A protective marking named in general content is written without initial capitals, or a reported marking's capitalisation differs from its actual appearance.
context_preconditions: Use initial capitals for references to protective markings in general content.
When reporting how a marking actually appears on a page, preserve its actual capitalisation instead.
Checking the reporting exception requires access to the marking being reported.
compliant_examples: Only those with an existing Negative Vetting 1 security clearance are considered for supervised temporary access to Top Secret information.
The field report was stamped ‘TOP SECRET’.

heading_path: Include a title page and preliminary parts
rules.statement: Give each image a page number in the list.
rules.body_excerpt:
Include a list of images and tables if it is helpful to the user.

Images can include photographs, figures and maps. Most reports only need a list of images and tables.

Give each image a page number in the list. In print, include even full-page images that don’t have a visible page number.

The order of lists is:

1. photographs (only in print)
2. figures
3. maps (if listed separately)
4. tables.
rules.violation_condition: An image's entry lacks a page number, or a printed report omits a full-page image from the list because its page number is not visible.
context_preconditions: The report has a list of images and page numbers.
In print, full-page images remain in the list even if their page number is not visibly printed.

heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
rules.statement: Always use an initial capital for 'the Treasury' to show the difference from its generic reference.
rules.body_excerpt:
The Department of Finance owns the policy. The Department has been working on it for months.

Always use an initial capital for ‘the Treasury’ to show the difference from its generic reference.
rules.violation_condition: The government organisation referred to as ‘the Treasury’ is written with a lower-case ‘t’.
context_preconditions: The reference is to the government organisation, not a generic treasury.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
compliant_examples: The Treasury conducts itself to the highest standards.

heading_path: Refer to the table in the text
rules.statement: Don't refer to 'the table below' or 'the table above'.
rules.body_excerpt:
Tables support the discussion in the text, not the other way around. It is essential to refer to a table in the text.

A single table on a webpage does not need a table number. If you use tables repeatedly, number tables and include the table number when you refer to the table in the text.

When using a table:

- Place the table close to where you mention it in the text and after the paragraph that refers to it. In print, the table should be on the same or facing page.
- Ensure that the table number referenced in the text matches the table number in the title.
- Don’t repeat the whole title of the table in the text.
- Don’t refer to ‘the table below’ or ‘the table above’.
- Ensure that the information in the text is consistent with the information in the table.

Your text comments on or interprets the table. Where possible, avoid repeating the text or data in the table word for word.
rules.violation_condition: A table reference identifies the table as ‘the table below’ or ‘the table above’.

rules.statement: 'previous names' instead of 'maiden name'.
rules.body_excerpt:
When you write to or about people, always use the form of personal name that the person uses. If you can, ask the person which name they prefer. Otherwise, consult reputable sources for:

- Names of people who work within government or in roles related to government, including state and territory governments: [Directory.gov.au](https://www.directory.gov.au/).
- Records of names of people closely associated with Australia: The [National Archives of Australia](https://www.naa.gov.au/help-your-research/getting-started/commonwealth-record-series-crs-system).
- Historical and biographical information: The [*Australian dictionary of biography*](http://adb.anu.edu.au/) and [Trove](https://trove.nla.gov.au/).
- Information on prominent Australians, search ‘eResources’ such as *Who*’*s who in Australia* or *Encyclopedia Britannica:* [National Library of Australia](https://www.nla.gov.au/)*.*
- The accepted form of authors’ names and the names of people being written about: library catalogues.

Names are important to a person’s sense of self. To avoid cultural or gender bias when referring to parts of names, use:

- ‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’
- ‘family name’ instead of ‘surname
rules.violation_condition: The term ‘maiden name’ is used to refer to a person's previous name.
context_preconditions: Applies when referring to this part of a personal name, rather than discussing or quoting the terminology itself.
Asking people for their names (forms, questions) is the cultural-diversity rule's (44cac46ea91ba0c2); this rule covers other references, so one form label is not flagged twice.
